title: Mowgli's Brothers
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
One night, a hungry tiger named Shere Khan came near a family of wolves. He was hunting people, but the human family escaped. Their baby crawled into the wolves’ cave. Mother Wolf called him Mowgli and protected him. Shere Khan returned and demanded the child. Mother Wolf refused. She said the baby belonged with her family now. Father Wolf agreed to raise him.

At the wolves’ meeting, Shere Khan argued that Mowgli should be given back. The young wolf leader listened. Under the Law of the Jungle, two members of the pack could speak for a cub who had no wolf parents. Baloo, a brown bear who taught the cubs, promised to teach Mowgli. Bagheera, a black panther, offered a freshly killed bull as a gift. The pack accepted the boy.

Mowgli grew up among the wolves. Baloo taught him the words and rules that helped animals live together. Bagheera showed him how to watch, listen, and move quietly. Mowgli learned quickly, but Shere Khan still hated him. The tiger waited for a chance to take him.

When Mowgli was older, Bagheera warned him that the pack’s old leader was becoming weak. Shere Khan was persuading younger wolves to forget their laws. Mowgli needed to face the danger. Bagheera told him to bring the red flower from the village, because fire frightened the animals. Mowgli went toward the human homes. He did not know whether he would stay with the wolves forever, but he knew that he had to protect the family that had raised him.

B1.text:
In the forest, a tiger named Shere Khan was hunting when a human family escaped from him. Their baby wandered into a wolf cave. Mother Wolf chose to keep the child and named him Mowgli. Shere Khan came to the entrance and demanded his prey. She stood between the tiger and the baby. Father Wolf also decided that Mowgli would grow up with their cubs.

At the pack’s meeting, Shere Khan complained that the humans’ child did not belong among wolves. The Law of the Jungle allowed two outsiders to speak for a cub. Baloo, the bear who taught young animals, offered to teach Mowgli. Bagheera, the panther, gave the pack a bull he had killed. The wolves accepted both the gift and the promise, so Mowgli became part of the pack. Mother Wolf stands between the tiger and the cave entrance. Father Wolf watches the child, who reaches for the warm fur beside him instead of crying. At the meeting, the wolves listen as Baloo offers to teach him and Bagheera offers a bull. Only then do they agree that Mowgli may stay.

As the boy grew, he learned the animals’ languages, paths, and customs. Baloo taught him the rules that kept the jungle peaceful. Bagheera showed him how to notice danger before it was close. Mowgli was clever and brave, though he sometimes forgot that he was smaller than the animals around him. Shere Khan continued to watch him and waited for the moment when the wolves would leave him unprotected.

Years later, Bagheera explained that the pack’s old leader was losing his strength. Shere Khan was using this change to turn the younger wolves against Mowgli. The panther urged the boy to find fire, which the animals feared, and to return prepared. Mowgli went toward the village to bring back the red flower. He felt pulled between two homes: the people he had not known and the wolf family that had raised him. He understood that the coming choice would change his place in the jungle.

A1.text:
A tiger came near a wolf family at night. A small boy crawled into their cave. Mother Wolf called the boy Mowgli and kept him safe.

The tiger wanted Mowgli, but Mother Wolf said no. The wolves met to talk about the boy. Baloo the bear said he would teach Mowgli.

Bagheera the panther brought food for the wolves. The pack let Mowgli stay with them. He grew up with the wolf cubs.

Baloo taught him the rules of the jungle. Bagheera taught him to watch and listen. But the tiger still wanted to hurt him.

One day Bagheera said the pack was changing. Some young wolves listened to the tiger now. Mowgli went toward the village to find fire.

title: Kaa’s Hunting
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Mowgli had gone looking for excitement, even though Baloo had warned him not to trust the Bandar-log, the noisy monkeys. The monkeys had no laws and often made promises they forgot. They watched Mowgli while he was alone, then carried him high into the trees. Mowgli called to them, but they only laughed and ran across the branches.

The monkeys took Mowgli to an old place among broken buildings. They wanted him to teach them how to build shelters and make plans. Mowgli knew they had taken him against his will. He tried to stay calm and sent a message through birds to Baloo and Bagheera. The two friends hurried after him, but the monkeys moved too quickly through the trees.

Baloo and Bagheera knew they needed help. They found Kaa, a very large python who could climb and move silently. Kaa listened to their story. The monkeys were afraid of him, but he agreed to help because Mowgli was in danger. Together they reached the old buildings. Baloo and Bagheera distracted the monkeys while Kaa climbed over the walls.

Kaa moved his body in a slow, powerful pattern. The monkeys could not stop watching him. They became confused and lost their courage. Kaa found Mowgli and carried him away from the ruins. Baloo and Bagheera followed. Mowgli was tired and sore, but safe. His friends reminded him that curiosity was not a reason to ignore every warning. Mowgli understood that his choices had put them all in danger, and he thanked them for coming.

Baloo and Bagheera knew they needed help. They found Kaa, a very large python who could climb and move silently. Kaa listened to their story. B1.text:
Baloo had warned Mowgli that the Bandar-log were unreliable, but the boy was curious about them. When he wandered away, the monkeys seized him and carried him across the treetops. They wanted him to show them how to build and make plans. Mowgli knew they were not listening to him. He sent a message to his friends with a bird and waited for help.

Baloo and Bagheera hurried after the monkeys. They could not move through the branches as quickly as the Bandar-log, so they searched for someone who could. They found Kaa, an old python whose size and quiet movements made the monkeys nervous. Kaa heard that Mowgli had been taken and agreed to join the rescue. The three animals followed the trail to a ruined human settlement.

The monkeys kept Mowgli among the broken walls. They talked about making him their teacher, but they could not agree on a plan. Baloo and Bagheera drew some of them away while Kaa climbed into the ruins. The python used a slow, steady movement that held the monkeys’ attention. Their confidence disappeared. Kaa reached Mowgli and helped him escape. From high in the trees, Mowgli sees the ruined city grow nearer. The monkeys pass him from branch to branch while he looks for a way down. At the old buildings they boast about their plans but forget them almost at once. Mowgli waits behind the broken walls, listening for Baloo and Bagheera.

Once they were beyond the ruins, Mowgli thanked the rescuers. Baloo and Bagheera were relieved, but they also explained why they had warned him about the monkeys. Mowgli had wanted to discover something new and had ignored the danger. His curiosity had become a problem for everyone who cared about him. He learned that courage does not mean refusing advice. A person can be curious and still listen carefully, especially when friends explain a real risk.

A1.text:
Baloo told Mowgli to stay away from the monkeys. They made promises and then forgot them. But Mowgli wanted to see where they lived.

The monkeys took Mowgli high into the trees. They carried him to some old, broken buildings. Mowgli wanted to go home, but they said no.

Mowgli sent a message with a bird. Baloo and Bagheera came to look for him. The monkeys ran quickly from tree to tree.

The two friends asked Kaa the snake for help. Monkeys were very afraid of Kaa. He came with Baloo and Bagheera to the buildings.

Kaa climbed over the wall and found Mowgli. The monkeys watched the big snake and grew quiet. Mowgli went home with his friends, tired but safe.

title: Tiger! Tiger!
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
After Mowgli was sent away from the wolf pack, he walked to a human village. The villagers were surprised by the boy from the forest. Messua welcomed him because he looked like the son she had lost. Mowgli stayed in her home and began to learn human ways. He wore clothes, ate meals at a table, and practiced the village language. He was kind to Messua, but village life felt strange to him.

The villagers asked Mowgli to watch their cattle. While he was away, Buldeo told stories about Shere Khan, the tiger who hunted nearby. Mowgli already knew the tiger and learned that Shere Khan still planned to kill him. He spoke with his wolf brothers and made a plan. The cattle would enter a narrow valley from both ends and trap the tiger.

Shere Khan was resting in the valley after eating. Mowgli and the wolves led the herds toward him. The frightened cattle rushed forward, and the tiger could not escape. Mowgli found that the danger had ended. He took the tiger’s skin as proof that Shere Khan would not threaten him again.

When Mowgli carried the skin into the village, the people became afraid. They thought he had used magic and chased him away. Messua had cared for him, but she could not change the villagers’ minds. Mowgli returned to the forest with his wolf brothers. He had learned how humans lived, yet their fear meant he could not stay. He would have to decide later where he belonged.

B1.text:
When Mowgli left the wolf pack, he made his way to a human village. The villagers had never met a boy who had grown up among animals, so they looked at him with suspicion. Messua, however, believed that Mowgli might be her lost child. She brought him into her home and taught him ordinary human customs: wearing clothes, eating at a table, and speaking with people. Mowgli appreciated her kindness, although he still felt most at ease outdoors.

The village gave him the task of watching its cattle. Buldeo, an older storyteller, spoke often about Shere Khan, the tiger that lived nearby. He assumed Mowgli knew nothing about the forest. Mowgli learned from his wolf brothers that the tiger was still looking for him. Together they planned to use the valley’s shape to trap Shere Khan between two herds.

The tiger had eaten and was sleeping in the valley. Mowgli guided one group of cattle while his wolf brothers brought another from the opposite end. The animals rushed forward, leaving Shere Khan no clear escape. The danger to Mowgli was over. He took the tiger’s skin, hoping the villagers would understand that the threat had ended. Mowgli waits until the cattle can be driven from two sides of the valley. The wolves help him move the herds, and the sleeping tiger has no open path between them. Afterward Buldeo wants to claim the tiger skin, but Mowgli refuses to let him take the result of the wolves’ work.

Instead, the villagers were frightened by Mowgli and accused him of using magic. They forced him to leave. Messua had offered him a place in her family, but she could not make the others trust him. Mowgli returned to the jungle with the wolves. His time in the village had taught him human habits, but it had also shown him how fear can separate people. For now, the forest was the only home where he could live freely.

Mowgli wore clothes and ate at a table. But he missed the forest and his wolf brothers. The people asked him to watch their cattle.

Mowgli heard that the tiger still wanted him. He made a plan with the wolves. They would take the cattle into a small valley.

The tiger lay there after a big meal. Cattle came from both sides of the valley. The tiger could not get away from them.

Mowgli took the tiger’s skin back to the village. The people feared him and made him leave. Mowgli went back to the forest with the wolves.

title: The White Seal
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Kotick was a young seal born on an island where many seals gathered each year. He was different from the others because his fur was white. At first, the other seals stared at him, but his mother cared for him. Kotick grew strong and enjoyed swimming in the sea.

One day he saw hunters arrive. They drove seals across the beach and killed many for their skins. Kotick was shocked. He tried to warn the other seals, but the adults believed that the hunting would always happen. They told him that the island was their home and that he should stop worrying.

Kotick could not accept this answer. He traveled through the ocean to look for a safe place. He met many sea animals and visited faraway shores. Some beaches were beautiful, but people came there too. Kotick kept going. He learned how to swim through deep water and how to find food in different places. The journey was long, and more than once he wondered whether a safe island existed.

At last Kotick found a hidden beach protected by rocks and difficult waves. People could not easily reach it. He returned to his home island and told the other seals what he had discovered. They did not believe him immediately. Kotick challenged them to follow him and see for themselves. The seals swam behind him across the sea. When they reached the quiet beach, they understood why he had kept searching. Kotick had found a place where their young could grow without hunters.

B1.text:
Kotick was born among a large group of seals that returned each year to an island. His white coat made him unlike the other young seals, but his mother cared for him. He learned to swim, hunt for fish, and rest on the shore. He believed the island was a safe place until he saw what the hunters did.

Men arrived and drove the seals into groups. They killed many animals for their skins. Kotick was frightened by the sight and tried to tell the adults what had happened. The older seals explained that the hunters had come for years. They thought nothing could change and advised Kotick to accept the danger. He could not agree. If the same thing happened each season, the young seals would never be safe.

Kotick began a long search through the ocean. He asked sea creatures about other islands and explored distant coasts. He learned that a beach might look peaceful but still be visited by people. His journey tested his strength. He swam through rough water, searched for food, and continued even when he had not found a safe home. He became more certain that he had to keep looking, because the old island offered no protection. Kotick swims far from the crowded island and asks other sea animals where seals can live without hunters. Some places have food but no safe shore; others are easy for boats to reach. He keeps searching even when the older seals tell him that no new home exists. At last he follows a path beneath the water to the hidden beach.

Eventually Kotick reached a sheltered beach surrounded by rocks and strong waves. It was difficult for people to land there, and the seals could rest without being disturbed. Kotick returned to his community and described the place. The adults doubted him, so he invited them to follow his route. When the seals reached the hidden shore, they saw that his search had found a real answer. Kotick’s patience gave the group a chance to live more safely.

Kotick was a young seal with white fur. He lived on an island with many seals. His mother taught him to swim in the sea.

One day men came to the beach. They took many seals away and killed them. Kotick was afraid for his seal friends.

The older seals said they could not change this. But Kotick wanted a safe home for everyone. He swam away to look for one.

Kotick saw many beaches and met sea animals. Some places looked good, but people went there too. He kept swimming and looking for a safe beach.

At last he found a beach behind hard rocks. The men could not come there easily. Kotick led the other seals to their new home.

title: Down the Rabbit-Hole
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Alice sat beside her sister on a warm day. Her sister’s book had no pictures, and Alice grew bored. Then a White Rabbit ran past. It looked at a watch and said that it was late. Alice had never seen a rabbit with a watch. She followed it across the field and into a hole under a hedge.

The hole became a deep tunnel. Alice fell for a long time. She saw shelves, maps, and jars along the walls. She took a jar marked orange marmalade, but it was empty. She put it back because she did not want it to fall on anyone below. As she fell, she wondered where she would land and thought about her cat Dinah at home.

At last Alice landed on dry leaves. She was not hurt. She ran after the Rabbit into a hall lit by lamps, but it vanished around a corner. Doors stood all around her, and each one was locked. On a little glass table she found a gold key. It opened a tiny door behind a curtain. Beyond the door was a garden with bright flowers, but Alice was too large to enter.

A bottle on the table said “DRINK ME.” Alice checked that it was not marked poison, then drank from it. She became small enough for the door, but the key was now high above her on the table. Alice tried to climb a slippery leg of the table and could not reach it. She sat down and cried. Then she found a little cake with “EAT ME” written on it. She ate the cake and waited to see what would happen.

B1.text:
Alice was sitting beside her sister on a hot afternoon when a White Rabbit hurried past. It spoke about being late and drew a watch from its pocket. Alice had seen rabbits before, but never one carrying a watch. She ran after it across the field and saw it disappear down a hole beneath a hedge. Without stopping to consider how she would return, she followed.

The tunnel dropped into a deep shaft. Alice fell slowly enough to notice maps, shelves, and cupboards in its walls. She picked up a jar labelled orange marmalade, discovered it was empty, and placed it safely in a cupboard as she passed. During the long fall she wondered how far she had travelled and whether her cat Dinah would miss her supper. Then she landed on a pile of dry leaves without being hurt.

The Rabbit was still ahead of her, so she chased it into a hall with a row of lamps. It vanished around a corner. Alice tried every door in the hall and found them locked. A small gold key lay on a glass table. At first none of the doors seemed to fit it, but then she noticed a low curtain. Behind it was a door hardly large enough for her head. The key opened this door, and Alice saw a garden filled with flowers and fountains. She could not squeeze through.

She found a bottle marked “DRINK ME” and checked that it did not say poison. After she drank, she shrank to the right size but realized she had left the key on the table. Its smooth legs were too slippery to climb. Alice cried for a while, then noticed a small cake marked “EAT ME.” She ate it, hoping that another change of size might help her reach the garden.

A White Rabbit ran past with a watch. He said he was late for something. Alice followed him into a deep hole. The Rabbit went ahead and Alice could not see him.

Alice fell for a long, long time. She saw maps and jars on the walls. Then she landed on dry leaves.

She ran into a hall with many doors. A small key opened one little door. Alice saw a beautiful garden, but she was too big. The little key lay on a glass table.

She drank from a bottle and became small. Now the key was too high to reach. Alice found a cake and ate it.

title: The Pool of Tears
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
After Alice ate the cake, she grew and grew. Her head nearly touched the ceiling. She could take the gold key from the table, but now she was far too big for the garden door. She lay on the floor and looked through the small opening. She felt upset and cried until a pool of tears spread across the hall.

The White Rabbit came back carrying gloves and a fan. He was in a hurry to see the Duchess. When he saw Alice, he dropped the things and ran away. Alice picked up the fan. As she held it, she began to shrink. She put it down quickly, afraid that she might become too small to find. Now she could move through the hall again, but she had lost the key.

Alice slipped into the pool she had made when she was large. She had to swim. At first she thought the water might be the sea. Then she saw a Mouse swimming nearby. Alice tried to speak politely and asked for help. She mentioned her cat Dinah, but the Mouse did not want to hear about cats. Alice said she would not speak of cats again. Then she mentioned a dog, and the Mouse swam away in anger.

Alice called the Mouse back and promised to avoid both subjects. It agreed to talk when they reached the shore. More animals and birds entered the pool, including a Duck, a Dodo, a Lory, and an Eaglet. They were all wet and tired. Alice swam toward the edge, and the others followed her out of the water.

B1.text:
The cake made Alice stretch so quickly that she wondered how she would ever reach her own feet. Her head struck the roof of the hall. She picked up the gold key, but the garden door was much too small again. She could only lie beside it and look through. Tears rolled down her face and made a pool across the floor.

The White Rabbit passed through the hall carrying gloves and a fan for the Duchess. Startled by the enormous girl, he dropped them and hurried away. Alice picked up the fan. She soon noticed that she was shrinking and released it before she became smaller still. She looked for the little door but could no longer find the key. Then she slipped into the water she herself had cried into the hall.

Alice swam through the pool, wondering for a moment whether she had fallen into the sea. A Mouse was swimming nearby. She tried to ask it for help, but talked about Dinah, the cat she loved at home. The Mouse was frightened and offended. Alice apologized and promised not to mention cats. When she then spoke of a dog she knew, the Mouse swam away again. She called after it and agreed to avoid both animals. As Alice swims, she tries several words to make the Mouse trust her. Speaking French makes the trouble worse because the word she remembers is about a cat. She says she is sorry and tries to change the subject. The Mouse agrees to explain itself once they are out of the water, so Alice stays close as they head for shore.

The Mouse returned and offered to explain its dislike when they were safely on land. More birds and animals joined them in the water: a Duck, a Dodo, a Lory, and an Eaglet. Their fur and feathers were soaked. Alice led the way toward the shore, and the strange group followed. They had escaped the pool, but none of them was dry yet.

A1.text:
Alice ate a cake and grew very big. Now she could get the key again. But she was too big for the little garden door.

Alice cried, and her tears made a pool. The White Rabbit came with a fan. He ran away and left the fan behind. The fan fell beside her on the floor.

Alice picked up the fan and grew small. She fell into the pool of her own tears. She had to swim to get out.

A Mouse swam beside Alice in the water. Alice spoke about her cat Dinah. The Mouse did not like hearing about cats. Alice asked the Mouse how to leave.

Alice said she would stop talking about cats. Birds and other animals came into the pool. They all swam together toward the shore.

title: A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
After climbing out of the pool, Alice and the animals stood on the bank. They were cold and wet. The dodo suggested a race to help them dry. He marked no starting point and gave no clear directions. The animals ran around the shore in many different ways. After a while, the dodo stopped them and announced that the race was finished.

The animals asked who had won. The dodo thought for a long time and said that everyone was a winner. Alice liked this answer. She had a few small sweets in her pocket and gave one to each animal as a prize. They thanked her, and for a moment the group felt cheerful.

The mouse then offered to tell a story. He wanted to explain why he was annoyed with a dog and a person. Alice tried to listen carefully. The mouse told it in a serious way, but Alice could not follow all of it. She asked questions and sometimes thought of other things. When she mentioned Dinah, her cat, the animals became uncomfortable. Alice praised Dinah for catching mice, and the mouse hurried away.

The mouse was upset with Alice and left. Alice called after him, but he did not come back. She tried to tell the other animals how gentle Dinah was at home. This made matters worse. The birds knew that a cat could catch them too, so one by one they found reasons to go away. Soon Alice was sitting alone beside the pool. She missed Dinah and wished she had not spoken about hunting. Then she heard the White Rabbit nearby. He was still worried about being late and was looking for something he had lost.

B1.text:
Once Alice and the animals reached the bank, they were soaked and shivering. The dodo proposed a race, believing that movement would dry them. He made no track and explained no rules. The animals ran around the shore whenever they chose, so there was no obvious beginning or end. Eventually the dodo called them back and announced that the race was over.

They asked who had won. After considering the question, the dodo declared that everyone should receive a prize. Alice agreed and handed out small sweets she had saved in her pocket. The animals were pleased, and the strange contest ended happily even though nobody had followed a shared plan. The dodo asks Alice to give the prizes, and she searches her pockets for enough sweets. When she has handed them out, the animals ask the dodo for a prize for Alice too. It takes a small thimble from her and presents it back to her with great ceremony. Alice accepts it as seriously as she can.

The mouse offered to tell a story about a dog and a person who disliked cats. Alice tried to listen, but she found the story difficult to follow. She interrupted with questions and sometimes let her thoughts wander. Then she began talking about Dinah, her own cat, and explained that Dinah was good at catching mice. The animals heard this as a frightening reminder of danger. The mouse left, and the others soon followed.

The mouse moved away before Alice could explain herself. She turned to the other animals and tried to praise Dinah, but describing a cat that caught birds frightened them too. One said it had to go home, and the rest soon followed. Alice called for them to stay, then found herself alone on the bank. She thought of Dinah at home and wished she could see her, although she now understood why her new companions did not want to hear about her. Before long the White Rabbit came by, hurrying and searching for something he had lost.

A1.text:
Alice and the animals came out of the pool. Their fur and feathers were all wet. The Dodo said a race could dry them.

Everyone ran in a different way. Nobody knew where the race should start. At last the Dodo said everyone had won. There was no line for the runners to follow.

Alice gave the animals small sweets. Then the Mouse began a long story. Alice tried to listen to every word.

Alice spoke about her cat Dinah again. The Mouse was upset and went away. Alice called after him, but he did not come back. Alice wished Dinah could be with her.

The birds left too, one after another. They were afraid a cat might catch them. Alice sat alone and heard the White Rabbit nearby.

title: The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Alice reached a small house and met the White Rabbit again. He thought she was his servant, Mary Ann, and ordered her to fetch his gloves and a fan. Alice went inside because she was curious and wanted to understand what was happening. She found the gloves and fan in a room upstairs. She picked up the fan, and soon she began to feel a familiar change: she was growing.

Alice grew so large that her body filled much of the little house. She could no longer stand comfortably. The White Rabbit looked through the window and became frightened. He called for help. A lizard named Bill was sent down the chimney to discover what was inside. Alice pushed him away with her foot, and he flew out of the chimney. The animals outside ran about in confusion.

The rabbit and his helpers tried to get Alice out. They threw small stones through the window. The stones changed into little cakes when they landed. Alice ate one and began to shrink. When she became small enough, she ran out of the house and escaped into the garden.

Outside, Alice found herself among tall plants and strange paths. A large puppy came toward her, playful but much bigger than she was. Alice used a stick to distract it and then moved away safely. She continued on, unsure which path would lead to the garden. The rabbit had treated her like a servant, but Alice had learned that following someone’s orders without understanding them could place her in a difficult situation.

B1.text:
At a small house, Alice met the White Rabbit. He mistook her for his servant and told her to bring his gloves and fan. Alice went inside, partly because she wanted to help and partly because she was curious. She found the objects upstairs. After picking up the fan, she began to grow again. The rooms were far too small for her changing body.

The White Rabbit looked in through a window and panicked. He called for help. His servant Bill, a lizard, was sent down the chimney to investigate. Alice pushed him away, and Bill came flying out. The animals gathered outside were confused and frightened by the enormous girl inside the house. When Bill is sent down the chimney, Alice hears him moving above her. She kicks upward, and a crash outside tells her he has fallen into the garden. The Rabbit’s helpers gather around him while Alice looks for another way out. The little cakes made from stones soon shrink her enough to slip through the door.

The rabbit’s helpers tried several ways to remove Alice. They threw small stones through the window. As they landed near her, the stones became little cakes. Alice ate one and started to shrink. When she was small enough, she escaped from the house and reached the garden.

She soon encountered a puppy that was playful but huge beside her. Alice used a stick to distract it and moved out of its way. The encounter reminded her that even a friendly creature could be dangerous when there was such a difference in size. Alice continued along the garden paths, still unsure where she was going. The rabbit had assumed she would obey him, and she had acted before asking what he meant. Her choices had brought her into a tight situation. Now she was learning to pause, notice what was happening, and find a way out.

A1.text:
The White Rabbit saw Alice near his house. He thought she was a girl named Mary Ann. He told her to bring his gloves and fan.

Alice went upstairs and found his things. Then she started to grow very big. Soon the little house was too small for her. The little room grew crowded around her.

The Rabbit looked in and called for help. A small lizard named Bill came down the chimney. Alice pushed him out with her foot.

Animals threw little stones into the house. The stones became cakes on the floor. Alice ate one cake and grew small again. She wanted to find the garden again.

She ran outside before the Rabbit caught her. A big puppy came close to play. Alice used a stick and went safely away.

title: The Cyclone
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Dorothy lived with Aunt Em and Uncle Henry on a farm in Kansas. Their small house stood in a wide, flat place. The sun had dried the grass and the earth, and everything looked gray. Aunt Em worked hard and did not smile much. Uncle Henry worked in the fields. Dorothy’s little black dog, Toto, made her laugh as they played.

One day Uncle Henry looked at the sky and said a cyclone was coming. Aunt Em opened the trap door in the floor. A ladder led down to a shelter beneath the house. She called Dorothy to follow her. Toto ran under the bed instead. Dorothy went after him and picked him up, but before she could reach the trap door, the house shook.

The wind lifted the whole house into the air. Aunt Em had already gone into the shelter, and Uncle Henry was outside with the animals. Dorothy held Toto close. The house spun for a while, and the wind was very loud. Then it stopped shaking so much and moved through the air more gently. Dorothy could not see where it was taking them.

Hours passed. Toto ran about the room, but Dorothy grew tired. She lay on her bed and slept while the house travelled. At last a sudden bump woke her. The house had stopped moving. Dorothy looked around the familiar room, then went to the door. She opened it and saw green grass, beautiful trees, and bright flowers instead of the gray Kansas fields. She and Toto had reached a place they did not know.

B1.text:
Dorothy lived with Aunt Em and Uncle Henry in a small house on the Kansas prairie. The dry ground, grass, and sky seemed gray in every direction. Work and weather had made the adults serious, but Toto, Dorothy’s lively black dog, still made her laugh. Their house had only one room and a trap door leading to a shelter beneath it.

One afternoon Uncle Henry studied the sky and warned that a cyclone was coming. He hurried to look after the animals. Aunt Em opened the trap door and called Dorothy down the ladder. Toto hid under the bed. Dorothy crawled after him, and when she finally caught him, the house began to shake. She could not reach the shelter before the wind lifted the building.

The house spun, then rose high above the ground. Dorothy held Toto and waited. The noise outside was frightening, but after a while the room rocked less violently. She knew Aunt Em and Uncle Henry were no longer beside her. With no way to change the house’s course, she lay down on her bed and eventually fell asleep. Dorothy hears the storm grow louder around the house. The floor shakes while Toto runs from one corner to another. She tries to wait with him in her arms. After the house rises, its movement becomes surprisingly gentle, like a cradle rocking. The long ride gives her time to sleep before the sudden landing wakes her.

A hard landing woke Dorothy. The floor was still, and the wind had gone quiet. She opened the door expecting the same dry, gray country, but she saw green grass, trees, and flowers in many bright new colors. The view did not look like Kansas. Toto stepped near her, and Dorothy stood on the threshold, looking at the unfamiliar land where the cyclone had left them.

A1.text:
Dorothy lived on a farm with Aunt Em. Uncle Henry worked in the fields each day. Toto, her small dog, made Dorothy smile.

One day the sky grew dark and gray. Uncle Henry saw a big storm coming. Aunt Em went down to a room under the house. Aunt Em called Dorothy to the shelter.

Toto hid under the bed from the wind. Dorothy ran to get her little dog. The house began to shake before they could leave.

The wind lifted the house into the air. Dorothy held Toto and waited inside. After a long time, they both fell asleep. Toto ran around the room as they flew.

The house came down with a hard bump. Dorothy opened the door and looked outside. Green trees and bright flowers stood all around her.

title: The Council with the Munchkins
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Dorothy stood with Toto among the Munchkins. Their leader explained that the Wicked Witch of the East had controlled them for a long time. Dorothy’s house had landed on the witch, and the silver shoes now belonged to Dorothy. The Munchkins were happy to be free, but Dorothy felt worried. She had not meant to arrive in this country or become part of a fight between witches.

The people told her that another witch, the Wicked Witch of the West, was still powerful. Dorothy wanted to go back to Kansas. The Munchkins could not take her there, so they suggested she ask the Wizard of Oz. He lived in the Emerald City. The road to the city was marked with yellow bricks. Dorothy decided to follow it and take Toto with her.

Before she left, the Munchkins gave Dorothy a welcome and thanked her. The good Witch of the North placed a protective mark on her forehead. She also warned Dorothy not to remove the silver shoes. They might help her on the journey. Dorothy did not understand how important they were, but she kept them on.

At last Dorothy stepped onto the road. She was a visitor in a place she did not understand, but the Munchkins had treated her kindly. She knew she could not return to Kansas alone, so she began walking toward the Emerald City. She hoped the Wizard would know how to send her home. The road was the first clear direction she had received. Dorothy hoped the Emerald City would bring answers, and she kept the silver shoes safe as she walked away from the Munchkins.

B1.text:
The Munchkins gathered around Dorothy after the house landed. Their leader explained that the Wicked Witch of the East had ruled them. By landing on the witch, Dorothy had freed them. They were grateful, though Dorothy herself was unsettled. She had not planned to challenge a witch; she had only been caught in a storm.

The people told Dorothy that the Wicked Witch of the West remained dangerous. Dorothy wanted to return to Kansas, but the Munchkins did not know how to take her there. They recommended asking the Wizard of Oz, who lived in the Emerald City. To reach him, she could follow a road made of yellow bricks. Dorothy decided to try this route with Toto beside her.

Before she began, the people welcomed her and thanked her. The Good Witch of the North touched Dorothy’s forehead, leaving a protective mark. She also advised Dorothy to keep the silver shoes she had received from the witch of the East. Dorothy did not yet know what the shoes could do, but she followed the advice. The Good Witch explains that she cannot take Dorothy straight to Kansas. She points out the yellow road that leads toward the Emerald City. Dorothy looks down at her shoes and then at Toto, who has stayed beside her since the storm. The Munchkins watch her prepare to leave their land.

When Dorothy started along the road, she was leaving the only people she had met in this strange country. The Munchkins had helped her, and their kindness made her feel less alone. Still, she had a long way to go and no guarantee that the Wizard would grant her wish. She chose to keep moving because a chance of getting home was better than staying where she was. The yellow road gave Dorothy a practical next step. She had no map of the strange country, so she chose to trust the Munchkins’ directions and continue toward the city.

title: How Dorothy Saved the Scarecrow
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
As Dorothy walked along the yellow road, she passed a scarecrow standing in a field. He was made of straw and wore old clothes. His head was stuffed with straw, and a painted face showed a friendly smile. Dorothy was surprised when the scarecrow spoke. He said that he could not move because he was tied to a pole.

Dorothy climbed onto a fence and carefully lifted him down. The scarecrow felt happy to be free. He told her that he had no brain and wished he could think better. Dorothy explained that she was going to the Emerald City to ask the Wizard to help her return to Kansas. The scarecrow asked if he could come along and ask the Wizard for a brain.

Dorothy agreed. She thought that traveling with a friend would be better than walking alone. The scarecrow did not know much about the world, but he asked thoughtful questions. He wanted to understand how things worked. Dorothy and Toto told him about the farm and the storm. As they walked, they became a team.

The road led them through a wood. They took turns helping each other when the path was difficult. The scarecrow could see far ahead because he was tall, while Dorothy could solve ordinary problems. They believed the Wizard might help them both. Dorothy wanted a way home; the scarecrow wanted the ability to think. They continued toward the Emerald City together. The scarecrow thanked her again, and Toto walked around them. Dorothy felt less lonely with another traveler beside her. The Emerald City now seemed like a shared destination.

B1.text:
Dorothy followed the yellow road until she saw a scarecrow standing in a field. He was a figure made of straw and old clothes, fastened to a pole. When Dorothy came closer, he spoke to her. He asked for help because he could not climb down by himself.

Dorothy climbed onto a fence and pulled the scarecrow free. He was grateful and said he wished he had a brain. He believed that without one he could not think well. Dorothy told him that she was traveling to the Emerald City to ask the Wizard to help her return to Kansas. The scarecrow asked to join her and make his own request. The Scarecrow tells Dorothy about the crow that realized he could not frighten it. A farmer had made him to guard the corn, but birds soon learned he was only straw and old clothes. Dorothy listens while they walk. She thinks the Scarecrow has already noticed many things, even though he says he has no brain.

Dorothy welcomed him. She wanted company, and the scarecrow wanted to learn. Although he doubted his intelligence, he was curious and often asked questions that helped the group think about their situation. Dorothy described her farm and the storm that had brought her to this land. The scarecrow listened carefully as they walked.

Their different abilities made them useful companions. The scarecrow could look across the fields from his height, while Dorothy knew how to solve practical problems. Toto stayed close to them. They faced the road as a team, each hoping the Wizard could help. Dorothy still missed home, and the scarecrow still wanted a brain, but traveling together made the distance feel less difficult. The scarecrow’s company made the road feel less lonely. Dorothy still missed home, but she was glad that the Wizard’s city had become a shared destination.

He said he wanted a brain. Dorothy told him about the Wizard. She hoped the Wizard could send her home.

The Scarecrow asked to walk with her. He wanted to ask the Wizard for a brain. Dorothy said yes and called Toto to follow. Toto ran around their feet as they walked.

They walked into a wood together. The Scarecrow saw the road ahead. Dorothy helped when the path became hard to cross.

title: The Road Through the Forest
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Dorothy and the Scarecrow continued along the yellow road. The bricks became rough, uneven, and sometimes missing. The Scarecrow did not notice the holes. He stepped into them and fell, so Dorothy had to lift him back onto his feet. He laughed because he could not feel pain. At noon they rested beside a brook. Dorothy ate bread from her basket, but the Scarecrow did not need food because his mouth was only painted.

After lunch, the Scarecrow asked Dorothy about Kansas. She told him that the cyclone had carried her away and that the land at home was gray and dry. The Scarecrow could not understand why she wanted to leave the beautiful country around them. Dorothy said that home mattered to people, even when another place looked more beautiful. The Scarecrow had no brains, but he was curious about the world.

He told Dorothy how a farmer had made him only two days earlier. The farmer painted his face, filled his clothes with straw, and put him on a pole in a cornfield. The Scarecrow tried to walk away but could not touch the ground. Crows came to eat the corn because they knew he was only stuffed with straw. He began to wish for brains so he could think and understand things.

They walked on until the road entered a large, dark forest. The Scarecrow said they should follow it because it must lead somewhere. Dorothy held his arm when she could not see. He spotted a small cottage, and they went inside. Dorothy slept on a bed of dry leaves while the Scarecrow stood watch until morning.

B1.text:
The yellow road became rough after Dorothy and the Scarecrow had walked for several hours. Some bricks were uneven, broken, or missing. Dorothy and Toto went around the holes, but the Scarecrow walked straight ahead and repeatedly fell. He could not feel pain, so he laughed while Dorothy helped him stand again. At midday they rested beside a brook. Dorothy ate bread from her basket, while the Scarecrow explained that he could not eat because his mouth was painted and his head was filled with straw.

The Scarecrow asked Dorothy about Kansas. She described the gray prairie and explained that a cyclone had carried her away. He could not understand why she wanted to leave the beautiful land around them. Dorothy told him that people often prefer their own homes, even when another place seems more attractive. The Scarecrow listened and then told her about his short life. The path has holes where bricks are missing, and Dorothy sometimes has to help the Scarecrow over them. He tells her what the farmer and the crows said when he first stood in the field. She describes Aunt Em and Uncle Henry in Kansas. Their talk carries them along until the trees close over the road.

A farmer had made him only two days before. He painted the Scarecrow’s face, filled his clothes with straw, and placed him on a pole to frighten birds away from the corn. The Scarecrow tried to follow the farmer but could not reach the ground. Crows discovered that he was not real and ate the corn beside him. He felt useless and wished for a brain, believing that it would help him understand and act wisely.

By evening, Dorothy and the Scarecrow reached a forest where the branches covered the road. They continued in the dark. Dorothy held the Scarecrow’s arm because she could not see, while he searched for somewhere to rest. He found a small cottage. Dorothy slept on dry leaves, and the tireless Scarecrow stood quietly in a corner until morning.

He told her how a farmer made him. The farmer put straw inside old clothes. Crows ate the corn because they did not fear him. Dorothy ate from the basket she carried.

The road went into a dark forest. Dorothy held the Scarecrow’s arm there. They found a small house and stayed for the night.

title: Peter Breaks Through
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Wendy lived in London with her parents, her brothers John and Michael, and Nana, the dog who cared for the children. Mrs. Darling liked to hear what they had done each day. One evening she heard Wendy speak of a boy called Peter Pan. Wendy said Peter sometimes visited children in their dreams. Mrs. Darling remembered the name from when she was young, but she had never seen the boy.

The children talked about a place called Neverland. John imagined a boat, and Michael imagined adventures. Wendy seemed to know that Peter belonged there. Mrs. Darling listened to their stories, but she thought they were make-believe. She wondered why Wendy spoke of the boy as if he were real.

One morning Mrs. Darling found leaves on the nursery floor. They did not look like anything from the garden outside. Wendy said Peter Pan might have dropped them. Mrs. Darling did not believe her. She checked the window and the room, but she could not explain where the leaves had come from. Nana watched the nursery carefully.

That night Mrs. Darling fell asleep beside the children. She dreamed that Neverland was close to the room. Then the window opened, and a boy came in with a small bright light beside him. Mrs. Darling woke and saw him. She knew he was Peter Pan. Peter saw that she was an adult and moved toward the window. Before she could speak to him, he disappeared into the dark. Mrs. Darling was left in the nursery with a question she could no longer dismiss.

B1.text:
Wendy Darling lived with her parents, her younger brothers John and Michael, and Nana, the family dog who watched over the nursery. Mrs. Darling liked to learn what occupied the children’s minds. When she heard Wendy mention Peter Pan, she remembered stories about him from her own childhood. Wendy spoke as though the boy still visited children, although her mother had never met him.

Each Darling child imagined Neverland differently. John thought of exciting journeys; Michael wanted adventures of his own. Wendy described Peter as someone who belonged to that distant place. Mrs. Darling listened, uncertain how much was a game and how much the children believed. A boy who never grew older sounded impossible, yet Wendy seemed quite sure of his name.

One morning Mrs. Darling found leaves on the nursery floor. Wendy suggested that Peter had brought them, but the idea seemed absurd. The window was high above the street, and no ordinary child could climb through it. Mrs. Darling looked at the leaves again and could not find a simple explanation. Nana remained alert whenever the children were asleep. Nana finds the leaves before the children wake. Mrs. Darling studies them because they seem too fresh to have blown in from outside. Wendy insists that Peter came to the nursery, but her mother has only the children’s stories to go on. That night Mrs. Darling stays near their beds and watches the window.

Later Mrs. Darling dreamed that the island in the children’s stories had come near the house. The nursery window opened, and a boy appeared beside a moving point of light. She woke and saw him plainly. Something about him made her recognize Peter Pan at once. He noticed that she was grown up and escaped through the window before she could stop him. Mrs. Darling had heard her daughter’s stories, but now the unexplained visitor had entered the room itself.

A1.text:
Wendy lived with John and Michael in London. Their dog Nana watched them in the nursery. Mother came to hear their stories at night.

Wendy told Mother about a boy called Peter Pan. She said he came into children’s dreams. Mother knew the name but had never seen him.

The children talked about a place called Neverland. John thought of boats and Michael thought of games. Mother thought these stories were just dreams.

One morning Mother found strange leaves on the floor. Wendy said Peter might have left them. Mother looked at the window but found no answer.

That night a boy came through the window. A small light flew beside him in the dark. Mother woke, saw Peter, and watched him fly away.

title: The Shadow
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Mrs. Darling called for help when the strange boy came through the nursery window. Nana rushed in. The boy leaped back outside before the dog could catch him. Nana shut the window, but the boy’s shadow stayed behind. Mrs. Darling picked it up and looked at it carefully. She folded it and placed it in a drawer, hoping to learn who the visitor was.

The next days were busy in the Darling home. Mr. Darling wanted the children to behave well. One evening he told Michael to take his medicine. Michael refused because it tasted bad. Mr. Darling said he would take his own medicine too, but then he tried to avoid it. Nana was given medicine as well, and the children were upset when Mr. Darling treated her unfairly.

Mr. Darling felt foolish and angry. He said Nana would no longer sleep in the nursery. He took her outside and tied her in the yard. Wendy, John, and Michael wanted their dog back, but their father would not change his mind. Mrs. Darling worried as she prepared to go out with him.

Before leaving, Mrs. Darling checked the children. They were in their beds, and their small night lights were burning. Nana barked outside. Mrs. Darling thought of the boy at the window and the shadow she had hidden. She wanted to stay home, but the adults left for their evening visit. The nursery window was quiet for the moment, and Nana could not reach it from the yard.

B1.text:
When Mrs. Darling saw the boy in the nursery, she cried out. Nana rushed through the door, and the boy escaped through the open window. Nana closed it too late to catch him, but his shadow did not follow. Mrs. Darling found it left behind and examined it carefully. She folded it away, still wondering whether the visitor could really be Peter Pan.

At home the children soon had a different worry. Mr. Darling insisted that Michael take his medicine. To show how easy it should be, he offered to take his own dose, though he disliked it too. He tried to avoid swallowing it and then gave medicine to Nana. The children saw the unfairness and protested on the dog’s behalf. When Nana catches the shadow, Mrs. Darling folds it away where the children will not find it. She hopes to ask Peter about it if he returns. Later Michael watches his father avoid the same medicine he has ordered for the boy. The argument leaves everyone upset, and Nana can only bark when she is taken outside.

Mr. Darling became embarrassed and angry. He decided Nana should sleep outside instead of watching the nursery. Despite the children’s objections, he led her into the yard and tied her there. Mrs. Darling was uneasy. She remembered the unknown boy, the open window, and the shadow still kept inside the house. Nana had been the children’s guard at night, and now she could only bark from below.

That evening the parents were due to visit friends. Mrs. Darling looked once more at Wendy, John, and Michael in their beds. Their night lights burned beside them. Mr. Darling waited, and the couple finally left. Nana’s warning reached them from the yard, but they did not return. The shadow remained hidden in the nursery while its owner was free to come back for it.

A1.text:
Nana ran into the nursery after Peter came. Peter jumped out through the open window. His shadow stayed behind on the floor.

Mother put the shadow in a drawer. She wanted to ask Peter about it. But the family had other things to do. Nana could not come back into the room.

One night Michael did not want his medicine. Father said he would take his own medicine. Then he tried to put it off.

Father gave medicine to Nana too. The children were angry with him. Father took Nana outside and tied her there. Mother heard Nana call from outside.

Mother looked at the children in bed. Nana barked outside in the yard. Then Mother and Father went out for the evening.

title: Come Away, Come Away!
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
After Mr. and Mrs. Darling left home, a small bright fairy flew into the nursery. Her name was Tinker Bell. She opened drawers and searched for Peter Pan’s lost shadow. She was tiny enough to look in places that Peter could not reach easily. Peter came through the window and looked with her. When he found the shadow, he tried to stick it to his feet, but it would not stay. He pressed it down again, then watched it come loose. Peter sat down and cried.

The noise woke Wendy. Peter told her why he was upset, and she offered to help. She took a needle and thread and sewed the shadow back onto his feet. Peter was delighted. Wendy asked about his home. He told her of Neverland and the Lost Boys, children who lived there without parents. He had come to hear her stories for them.

Wendy’s brothers woke too. Peter asked the children to come with him. Wendy thought about her parents and Nana, but she wanted to see the place Peter described. Peter showed them how to fly. He said they needed happy thoughts and fairy dust. At first they tumbled and tried again. Soon they floated above their beds and around the nursery.

Outside, their parents hurried home because Nana was barking. Inside, Peter called the children toward the window. Wendy, John, and Michael flew out after him. Their parents entered the nursery a moment later. The beds were empty, and the open window looked out over the night sky.

B1.text:
Tinker Bell flew into the Darling nursery as soon as the parents had gone. The fairy searched drawers and pockets for Peter Pan’s lost shadow. Peter followed her through the window. When he found it, he tried to fasten it to himself, but it would not hold. He sat down in frustration, and his crying woke Wendy.

Wendy offered to sew the shadow back onto his feet. Peter stood still while she used needle and thread, then celebrated when he could move with his shadow again. He told Wendy about Neverland and the Lost Boys, who had no one to tell them stories. He had been listening at the nursery window because he liked the stories she told her brothers. Wendy wanted to know more about the place where he lived. Peter tries to press the loose shadow onto his feet with soap, but it falls away each time he moves. Wendy finds her needle and thread while he waits. After she finishes, Peter dances around the room. The younger boys wake to see him there, and soon all three children are trying to rise from the floor.

John and Michael woke. Peter invited all three children to leave with him. Wendy remembered her parents and Nana, yet she was drawn to the journey Peter described. He showed them how to lift off the floor with happy thoughts and fairy dust. Their first attempts were awkward. They rose, fell, and tried again until they could fly around the room.

Nana barked outside, and Mr. and Mrs. Darling hurried back toward the house. Peter heard that the adults were coming and urged the children to leave at once. Wendy, John, and Michael followed him through the window into the night. Their parents reached the nursery just after they had gone. The open window and empty beds told them how late they were.

A1.text:
A small fairy called Tinker Bell flew inside. She looked for Peter’s lost shadow. Peter came in through the window after her.

Peter found his shadow in a drawer. It would not stay on his feet. He sat down on the floor and cried. The shadow came loose when Peter moved.

Wendy woke up and helped Peter. She used a needle to sew his shadow on. Peter told her about the Lost Boys in Neverland.

John and Michael woke up too. Peter asked them all to come with him. He showed them how to fly with fairy dust. They went up toward the ceiling together.

The children flew around their room and laughed. Then they followed Peter out of the window. Mother and Father came home to find empty beds.

title: The Flight
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Peter led Wendy, John, and Michael toward Neverland. He gave them a strange direction: second to the right, then straight on until morning. The children tried to follow, although the way was hard to understand. They flew over the sea for a long time. On the second sea they reached their third night, and they began to feel cold and hungry. Peter chased birds and brought food to them. Still, he often rushed away because he wanted to have more adventures.

The journey made the children sleepy. Michael started to fall through the air, but Peter caught him just in time. Wendy was frightened and angry. Peter had not been watching the children closely. He taught them to float and sleep in a strong wind, then disappeared again to explore. Wendy and her brothers continued without knowing when he would return.

After many days and nights, they finally reached the island. It looked dark and dangerous from above. Peter pointed toward places where the Lost Boys lived and told them that Captain Hook and his pirates were there too. Wendy wanted to see the island, but she also thought about the home and parents they had left. She stayed close to John and Michael. They had arrived, but they still needed to understand the island and decide how to keep one another safe. The children could hear the wind around them. Wendy watched the boys and tried to remember the direction they had come from. She wanted to help her brothers, even when Peter was not nearby.

B1.text:
Peter gave Wendy, John, and Michael directions to Neverland: second to the right and straight on until morning. The route was difficult to follow, but they flew on. They crossed several seas, and by the third night over the second sea they were cold and hungry. Peter chased birds and brought the children food. He was quick and excited, but he also kept leaving them to follow his own adventures.

The long flight made everyone tired. Michael began to drop through the air while he slept. Peter caught him at the last moment. Wendy was upset that Peter had not been watching him. Peter showed the children how to float and sleep safely in a strong wind. Then he went away again. The others had to continue without knowing when he would come back. Peter often flies ahead and then forgets to look back. Wendy calls to her brothers when they drift apart in the dark. Tinker Bell’s little light helps them find Peter again. As the flight continues, the children grow hungry and tired, but Peter keeps talking about the island they will see below them.

Many days and nights passed before the island appeared below them. From above, it seemed dark and threatening. Peter pointed out where the Lost Boys might be and spoke about Captain Hook and his pirates. Wendy had wanted an adventure, but she now understood that the island could be dangerous. She missed the familiar nursery and her parents, and she kept John and Michael close. They had reached the place Peter called home, but they were newcomers. They would need to learn its dangers and care for one another instead of depending only on Peter. The children could hear the wind around them. Wendy watched the boys and tried to remember the direction they had come from. She wanted to help her brothers, even when Peter was not nearby.

Michael grew sleepy and began to fall. Peter caught him before he reached the water. Wendy asked Peter to watch her brothers.

Peter taught them to rest in the wind. Then he went away again for a while. Wendy stayed close to John and Michael. The island looked dark from the sky.

At last they saw Neverland below them. Peter spoke of Lost Boys and pirates there. Wendy looked at the island and thought of home.

title: A Scandal in Bohemia
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Dr. Watson visited his old friend Sherlock Holmes and found him speaking with a masked man. The visitor was the King of Bohemia. He feared that a photograph of him with Irene Adler could damage his reputation and his planned marriage. He asked Holmes to find the picture before Irene used it.

Holmes studied Irene’s habits and watched her house. He disguised himself as a worker and learned where she kept her important things. Watson helped him create a small distraction outside. When smoke seemed to come from the house, Irene hurried to a hiding place for the photograph. Holmes noticed exactly where she went.

Holmes returned later with Watson to take the picture. But Irene had already understood that he was watching her. She had disguised herself and followed him. She told Holmes that she had kept the photograph only to protect herself. She did not plan to harm the King unless he threatened her.

When Holmes and Watson returned, Irene had already left with the man she had married. She had left a letter for Holmes. In it she explained that she recognized his disguise and followed him to make sure of his plan. She also promised that she would keep the photograph with the King only for her own safety. The King was satisfied when he heard this. He offered Holmes an expensive ring, but the detective asked for the photograph Irene had left behind instead. Watson and Holmes went home without the picture they had searched for.

B1.text:
Dr. Watson visited Sherlock Holmes and found him with a disguised visitor: the King of Bohemia. The King feared that Irene Adler possessed a photograph that could damage his reputation and interfere with his marriage. He wanted Holmes to recover it before she could reveal it.

Holmes investigated Irene’s routine and studied the house. He disguised himself as a worker to observe her movements. Watson helped create a commotion outside. When smoke appeared to rise from the building, Irene ran to a hidden place for the photograph. Holmes saw where she kept it and believed he could retrieve it later. Holmes watches Irene enter a church with a man named Godfrey Norton. The two ask him to witness their marriage before he can leave. Later, outside her home, Watson follows Holmes’s signal and throws a smoke device toward the window. Irene runs to the hidden photograph, giving Holmes the clue he had sought.

However, Irene had recognized that Holmes was paying attention. She changed her appearance and followed him after he left. She told him that she kept the photograph as protection, not as a plan to harm the King. If he respected her privacy, she would not use it against him. She then left the country with the image.

By the time Holmes returned to Irene’s house, she and her new husband had gone. She had left a letter explaining how she recognized the disguised detective and followed him after the false fire alarm. Her photograph with the King was still in her possession, but she promised to use it only if he threatened her. She left another photograph of herself in its place. The King accepted this promise and offered Holmes an expensive ring. Holmes chose Irene’s own photograph instead. Watson watched his friend take the picture, aware that Irene had anticipated their next move.

A1.text:
Watson visited his friend Sherlock Holmes. A king came to ask them for help. A woman named Irene had a photo of him.

The king feared people would see the photo. Holmes went to watch Irene’s house. Watson helped him make a little noise outside. The photo could hurt the king’s new marriage.

Someone called out that there was a fire. Irene ran to where she kept the photo. Holmes saw the place and left.

When Holmes came back, Irene was gone. She had seen through his plan. A letter said she kept the photo for safety. Irene had sent Holmes a letter too.

The king was happy when he heard this. Irene would not show the photo to others. Holmes asked for her own photo as his gift.

title: The Red-Headed League
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Jabez Wilson, a shopkeeper with bright red hair, came to Holmes with a strange story. A group called the Red-Headed League had paid him to copy an encyclopedia every day. The work was easy, and the pay was good. Then one morning he arrived and found a notice saying the League had ended.

Holmes asked questions about Wilson’s shop and his assistant, Vincent Spaulding. Spaulding was willing to work for very little money and often disappeared into the cellar. Holmes looked at the assistant’s trousers and noticed marks on the knees. He also checked the bank near Wilson’s shop and learned that a safe was being kept there.

Holmes guessed that the League had been invented to keep Wilson away from his shop. While Wilson sat copying in another room, someone could dig a tunnel from the cellar toward the bank. Holmes and the police hid near the bank one evening. They waited until two men came through the tunnel. One was Spaulding, whose real name was John Clay.

When the two men climbed out of the tunnel, Holmes and the police caught them. Spaulding was really John Clay, a thief who had used the strange job to get Wilson out of the shop. Clay tried to escape but could not pass the officers. The bank’s money was still safe. Later Holmes explained the trick to Watson: the low wages Spaulding accepted, his visits to the cellar, and the worn knees of his trousers had led Holmes to the tunnel. Wilson could return to his shop, though he would receive no more pay from the League.

B1.text:
Jabez Wilson, a shopkeeper known for his bright red hair, asked Holmes about a job that had suddenly disappeared. The Red-Headed League had paid him to copy an encyclopedia for several hours each day. The work seemed simple and the wages were surprisingly good. One morning, he found a note saying the organization had closed.

Holmes asked about Wilson’s shop and his assistant, Vincent Spaulding. Spaulding accepted unusually low pay and often went into the cellar. Holmes noticed dirt on the assistant’s knees. He also learned that a bank was close to the shop and held a valuable safe.

Holmes suspected that the League had been created to keep Wilson away from his business. While Wilson copied text in another room, someone could dig from the cellar toward the bank. Holmes and the police waited there one night. Two men emerged through the tunnel. One was Spaulding, whose real identity was John Clay. Before the arrest, Holmes taps the pavement outside Wilson’s shop and looks at the buildings behind it. The bank is close enough for a tunnel to reach. That evening he brings Watson, a police officer, and a bank official into the cellar. They wait in the dark until the floor opens and the thieves come through.

When the tunnel opened, Holmes and the police seized the men climbing through it. Wilson’s assistant was John Clay, a wanted criminal who had used the League to make the shopkeeper leave his business every day. Clay protested, but the officers took him away before he could reach the bank’s money. Afterward Holmes walked Watson through the clues: Spaulding’s low wages made little sense unless he wanted access to the shop; his time in the cellar and the marks on his knees pointed to digging. The end of the copying job meant that the tunnel was nearly ready.

A shopkeeper named Wilson came to Holmes. A strange group paid him to copy words. Then the group suddenly closed.

Holmes asked about Wilson’s shop helper. The helper went down into the cellar often. Holmes saw dirt on the knees of his trousers. Wilson came to the closed room and found a note.

A bank stood next to Wilson’s shop. Holmes thought the helper dug under the ground. The copying job kept Wilson away all day.

Holmes and the police waited at the bank. Two men came up from a tunnel. One was the shop helper, a thief called Clay. The men had dug toward the bank’s safe.

The police caught Clay before he could run. The bank kept its money safe. Holmes told Watson how he had found the tunnel.

title: A Case of Identity
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Mary Sutherland came to Holmes because her fiancé, Hosmer Angel, had disappeared. She explained that Hosmer had been kind and careful. He asked her to write letters to him and said she should keep their engagement private. On the morning they planned to marry, he entered a carriage and vanished before it reached the church.

Holmes asked about Mary’s family. Her stepfather, James Windibank, did not want her to marry. He often traveled for work and had discouraged her from going out. Holmes noticed that Hosmer never met Mary in daylight and that his voice and appearance were unusual. He compared the letters and found that they had been typed.

Holmes realized that Hosmer Angel was not a real person. Windibank had disguised himself as Mary’s fiancé to keep her from meeting other men while he was away. He wanted Mary to remain at home because her money helped support the family. When he returned from travel, the disguise could disappear without explanation.

Holmes invited Windibank to his rooms and showed him what the typed letters revealed. Windibank did not deny the trick for long. He had dressed as Hosmer, used dark glasses, and changed his voice so Mary would not know him. He wanted her to promise to wait for Hosmer and avoid another marriage. Holmes was angry and reached for a whip, but Windibank ran away. Mary had already left the rooms before this meeting. Holmes did not tell her the answer. He told Watson that she would probably refuse to believe him if he did.

B1.text:
Mary Sutherland asked Holmes to find her fiancé, Hosmer Angel, who had vanished on the morning of their wedding. She described him as gentle and dependable. He had insisted that they keep the engagement secret and asked her to write letters because he could not always speak freely. At the church, he entered a carriage and disappeared before they arrived.

Holmes asked about Mary’s home life. Her stepfather, James Windibank, opposed her marriage and often traveled for work. Holmes found it unusual that Hosmer never met Mary in daylight. His voice and appearance also seemed carefully controlled. The letters Mary had received were typed, which made it harder to identify the writer. Mary brings the letters and describes the tinted glasses and quiet voice Hosmer used. Holmes listens to the dates of Windibank’s journeys and compares them with Hosmer’s visits. The pattern points to one person playing two roles. When Windibank later comes to Holmes’s room, Mary has already gone home.

Holmes concluded that Hosmer did not exist. Windibank had used a disguise to pose as Mary’s fiancé. He wanted her to remain unmarried and at home because her income supported the household. When his work trips ended, he could simply disappear as Hosmer and return as himself.

Holmes summoned Windibank and compared the typed letters with a sample from his office. The same faults appeared in the typewriter’s letters. Confronted with this evidence, Windibank could no longer hide that he had posed as Hosmer. By making Mary promise to remain faithful after her fiancé vanished, he hoped to keep her income in the household. Holmes threatened to take a whip to him, and Windibank fled the room. Mary was not present for the confrontation. Holmes chose not to tell her the solution, saying that she would not believe him. Watson heard the explanation after she had gone.

Her stepfather had dressed up as Hosmer. He wanted Mary to stay at home. He did not want her money to leave the family. The stepfather wore dark glasses in his disguise.

Holmes asked the stepfather to come and talk. The man ran away when Holmes knew his trick. Mary did not hear the answer from Holmes.

title: The Boscombe Valley Mystery
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
A young man named James McCarthy was accused of killing his father in a valley. The father had been found dead near a pool, and people believed James had argued with him. James said he was innocent. His fiancée, Alice Turner, asked Holmes to investigate because she did not believe he was guilty.

Holmes and Watson examined the place where the father had died. Holmes studied footprints, the ground, and the way the body had fallen. He found signs that another person had been nearby. The story seemed more complicated than the argument between father and son.

Holmes asked about the Turner family and learned that Alice’s father, John Turner, had known James’s father in Australia. Turner was very ill, but Holmes spoke with him privately. Turner admitted that he had killed McCarthy. Years earlier, both men had been involved in crime in Australia. McCarthy later used that knowledge to pressure Turner and demand that Alice marry James.

Turner wrote down his confession for Holmes. Holmes said he would use it if James could not be cleared in another way. He did not want Turner’s daughter to learn her father’s secret unless it was necessary. James’s case was later resolved without Holmes handing over the confession. Turner, already very ill, died some months afterward. Holmes and Watson left the valley knowing why the marks near the pool had not fitted the villagers’ first story. Alice and James could look ahead without the charge of murder hanging over him any longer.

B1.text:
James McCarthy was accused of killing his father near a pool in a valley. Witnesses knew that the two men had argued, so many assumed James was responsible. James denied it. Alice Turner, his fiancée, asked Holmes to examine the case because she believed the accusation was wrong.

Holmes and Watson visited the place where the body had been found. Holmes looked closely at footprints, marks in the soil, and the position of the body. The evidence suggested that someone else had been present. The argument between father and son was not enough to explain everything. At the pool, Holmes notices that the marks in the ground do not all belong to James and his father. He asks Watson to look again at the direction of the footprints. He also checks what the injured man was heard to say. These small clues lead him toward Turner before the confession confirms the story.

Holmes learned that Alice’s father, John Turner, had known the dead man when both were in Australia. Turner was seriously ill, but he spoke privately with Holmes. He admitted that he had killed McCarthy. In the past, the two men had taken part in crimes. McCarthy later used that history to threaten Turner and demand that Alice marry James.

Turner gave Holmes a written confession. Holmes promised to keep it private unless the court needed it to clear James. The other evidence helped free the young man, so Holmes did not have to reveal the confession. Turner died later from his illness. Alice and James could plan their future without a murder charge hanging over him, though they did not know every part of the older men’s history. Back in London, Holmes reviewed the scene with Watson, explaining how the footprints and the dying man’s words had pointed beyond the son whom everyone first suspected.

James was blamed for his father’s death. Alice said James had done nothing wrong. She asked Holmes to find the truth.

Holmes and Watson went to the valley. Holmes looked at marks near a pool. Another person had walked there too. People said James had fought with his father.

Holmes spoke with Alice’s father, Mr Turner. Turner knew James’s father from many years ago. The two men had a bad secret.

Turner said he had killed James’s father. He wrote this down for Holmes. Holmes kept the paper in case James needed it. Turner was afraid Alice would hear his secret.

James was freed without showing that paper. Mr Turner was very ill and soon died. Alice and James could live without the charge.

title: The Lion and the Mouse
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
A lion was sleeping in the shade when a small mouse ran across his paw. The lion woke and caught the mouse. He was angry that such a tiny animal had disturbed him. The mouse begged to be released. It promised that one day it might help the lion. The lion laughed because he could not imagine needing help from a mouse. Still, he opened his paw and let the little animal go.

Some time later, hunters came into the forest. They set a strong net to catch the lion. The lion stepped into it and became trapped. He roared loudly and pulled at the ropes, but the net held him. The mouse heard his cries and hurried over.

The mouse reached the net and looked at the thick ropes around the lion. It could not lift the net, but it could bite one strand at a time. The lion stopped pulling so the small animal could work. The mouse held a rope between its teeth and chewed until the strand broke. It moved to another and did the same thing. Slowly a hole opened. The lion pushed his head through it, then his shoulders. At last he stepped out onto the forest floor. The mouse was still beside the broken ropes. The lion looked down at the animal he had once held in one paw. He thanked it for coming when he called. The mouse reminded him of the day he had let it go. They left the hunters’ net behind, walking away from the place where the lion had been trapped.
