The mouse reached the net and looked at the thick ropes around the lion. It could not lift the net, but it could bite one strand at a time. The lion stopped pulling so the small animal could work. The mouse held a rope between its teeth and chewed until the strand broke. It moved to another and did the same thing. Slowly a hole opened. The lion pushed his head through it, then his shoulders. At last he stepped out onto the forest floor. The mouse was still beside the broken ropes. The lion looked down at the animal he had once held in one paw. He thanked it for coming when he called. B1.text:
A lion slept beneath a tree. A mouse ran over his paw and woke him. The lion caught the mouse and wanted to punish it for disturbing his rest. The mouse asked to be set free and promised that it might repay the lion one day. The lion thought this was funny: a small mouse could hardly help a powerful lion. But he chose to release it.

Later, hunters placed a net in the forest. The lion walked into it and became trapped. He pulled hard, but the ropes held him. His loud roars reached the mouse, which came to see what had happened. The mouse remembered that the lion had spared its life.

The mouse ran to the edge of the net while the lion pulled at it again. The ropes only tightened, so he held still and let the smaller animal work. The mouse chose a strand, bit through it, then began on the next. Its teeth were small, but they could cut where the lion’s paws could not reach. One by one the ropes gave way. When the gap was wide enough, the lion pushed his head and shoulders through and climbed free. He stood beside the mouse, looking back at the net that had held him. He thanked the animal whose promise he had once found amusing. The mouse had remembered the open paw and the chance to leave safely. Now the lion could walk away because the mouse had returned. The two left the broken net on the ground and went back into the forest. The mouse works slowly around the strongest knot. It pulls one loosened thread aside and bites the next. The lion stops struggling so the net will not tighten again. As more cords break, he can move one paw, then another. The little animal stays until there is space for him to crawl free.

A1.text:
A Lion slept under a tree. A little Mouse ran over his paw. The Lion woke up and caught it.

The Mouse asked the Lion to let it go. It said it might help him one day. The Lion laughed but opened his paw. The Lion did not think a Mouse could help.

Later some hunters put a net in the forest. The Lion walked into it and could not leave. He called out for help.

The Mouse heard his voice and came quickly. It bit the ropes with its small teeth. The Lion waited while the Mouse worked. The ropes were too strong for the Lion.

At last the net had a hole. The Lion stepped out and thanked the Mouse. A small friend had helped a big one.

title: The Wolf and the Lamb
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
A lamb was drinking from a clear stream. A wolf stood farther up the water. He saw the lamb and wanted an excuse to attack it. The wolf shouted that the lamb was making the water dirty. The lamb answered politely that it was drinking downstream, so it could not be sending mud toward the wolf.

The wolf then said that the lamb had insulted him the year before. The lamb explained that it was not yet born at that time. The wolf changed his complaint again. He said that if the lamb had not done it, one of its relatives must have. The lamb could not answer for someone else.

The wolf came closer to the lamb after each answer. The lamb pointed to the direction of the stream. The water ran from the wolf toward the lamb, not the other way round. That answer did not stop the wolf. When he spoke of the year before, the lamb said it had not even been born. The wolf changed his story again and spoke of the lamb’s family. The lamb could not tell him what any relative had said. It stood by the water with no more answers to give. The wolf had not been waiting for an explanation. He moved toward the lamb and attacked it. The clear stream continued to run past them. Nothing the lamb had said about the water or the earlier year had changed the wolf’s actions. He had made his decision before he asked the first question.

B1.text:
A lamb came to drink from a stream. A wolf stood upstream and wanted to catch it. He accused the lamb of making the water muddy. The lamb calmly explained that the water flowed from the wolf toward the lamb, so it could not have dirtied the wolf’s drinking place.

The wolf made a new accusation. He said that the lamb had spoken badly about him the previous year. The lamb pointed out that it had not been born then. The wolf changed the story again, claiming that a member of the lamb’s family must have insulted him. The lamb said it could not be responsible for something a relative might have done. The lamb does not move upstream while it answers. It stays where the water is clear and speaks carefully to the wolf. Each time the wolf makes a new claim, the lamb gives a simple reason it cannot be true. The wolf’s growls become louder, but the stream keeps flowing in the same direction.

The lamb tried once more to show the wolf where each of them stood beside the stream. Mud could not travel against the flow of water. The wolf did not look at the current. He stepped nearer and brought up the insult from the year before. When the lamb explained that it had not yet been born, he made a new claim about its family. The lamb could answer for its own words, not for an unknown relative. Its calm explanations became shorter as the distance between them closed. The wolf did not need to win the argument; he only wanted to make an attack sound deserved. He sprang at the lamb despite its answers. The water flowed on from the place where the wolf had stood to the place where the lamb had been drinking. The facts had remained plain even while his story kept changing.

A1.text:
A Lamb drank water from a stream. A Wolf stood farther up the stream. He wanted to hurt the Lamb.

The Wolf said the Lamb made his water dirty. The Lamb said the water ran the other way. Her answer was true. The Lamb stood below the Wolf in the water.

The Wolf said she had been rude last year. The Lamb said she was not born then. The Wolf found another reason.

He said someone in her family was rude. The Lamb could not speak for her family. The Wolf came closer and closer. She looked at the water as it ran by.

The Lamb had no more answers to give. The Wolf attacked her by the stream. He had wanted this from the start.

title: The Ass and the Grasshopper
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
An ass heard a grasshopper singing in the field. The music sounded light and beautiful. The ass asked what the grasshopper ate to make such a lovely song. The grasshopper said that it lived on dew, the tiny drops of water found on leaves in the morning.

The ass believed that the grasshopper’s food must be the reason for its music. It decided to eat only dew. The ass stopped eating the food it needed and waited for drops of water instead. At first it felt proud of copying the grasshopper. It hoped that it would soon sing in the same way.

Each morning the ass looked for drops on the grass and leaves. It lowered its head and licked up the dew, then waited for more. It returned to the same leaves, but found only a few tiny drops there. The grasshopper was small enough to live on very little, but the ass had a large body to feed. It grew hungry. When it tried to work, its legs felt weak. It listened for its own voice, hoping that the song would come, but it could not sing like the grasshopper. The other animal had not told it to give up its usual food. The ass had decided to do that by itself after hearing the music. More mornings passed, and the little drops still were not enough. The ass had less strength each day. It could no longer do its ordinary work. The grasshopper’s song continued in the field while the ass lay weak nearby.

B1.text:
An ass listened to a grasshopper singing. The song was beautiful, and the ass wanted to know how the small insect could make such a sound. It asked about the grasshopper’s food. The grasshopper replied that it lived on dew, the water that gathers on plants.

The ass decided to eat only dew, believing this diet might help it sing. It stopped eating its usual food and waited for drops on the leaves. It copied the grasshopper’s habit without thinking about the difference between their bodies. A grasshopper is small and needs little food; an ass is much larger and needs nourishment to work. The grasshopper keeps eating what suits it while the ass waits for another morning of dew. The ass looks from one wet leaf to the next, finding only tiny drops. It leaves its usual food untouched. Day after day the difference between the small insect and the larger animal becomes harder for the ass to ignore.

The ass went out early to find dew on the leaves. It took small drops from the grass and waited for the sun to bring another morning. The grasshopper could sing after living on such a light diet, so the ass kept hoping for the same result. Its own large body needed more food. Hunger made it slow, and before long it could not work as it had before. It tried to make a beautiful sound, but the change in food had not changed its voice. The grasshopper had simply described its own life; it had not asked the ass to stop eating. The ass had made that choice alone without knowing whether dew could sustain it. Day after day it grew weaker. The singing insect remained in the field, while the animal that had admired its music struggled to stand and carry out ordinary tasks.

A1.text:
An Ass heard a Grasshopper sing. He wanted to make a song like that. He asked what the Grasshopper ate.

The Grasshopper said it drank drops from leaves. These little drops are called dew. The Ass thought dew made the song. The drops were very small in the morning.

The Ass stopped eating his usual food. Each morning he looked for drops on leaves. He drank a little and waited for more.

The Ass was much bigger than the Grasshopper. The drops did not give him enough food. He became hungry and could not work. The Ass still wanted a beautiful voice.

The Ass tried to sing, but no song came. His legs grew weak from too little food. The Grasshopper kept singing in the field.

title: The Wolf and the Crane
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
A wolf ate too quickly and got a bone stuck in his throat. He could not remove it with his paws, and the bone hurt when he swallowed. The wolf asked the other animals to help, but they were afraid of his sharp teeth. A crane had a long beak and neck, so the wolf asked it to reach inside his mouth and take out the bone.

The crane was nervous. The wolf promised to give it a reward if it helped. The crane carefully put its beak into the wolf’s mouth and pulled the bone out. The wolf could breathe and eat again. The crane then asked for the promised payment.

The crane pulled its long beak away from the wolf’s mouth as soon as the bone came free. It stepped back and watched him breathe normally again. Then it asked for the reward he had promised. The wolf opened his mouth, showing the teeth the crane had just passed. He said that the crane was lucky to have taken its head out safely. He would give it nothing else. The crane looked at the wolf for a moment. It had done exactly what he asked, but he would not keep his promise. It did not put its beak near him again or try to argue while standing beside his teeth. The bird walked away with its head safe. Behind it, the wolf could eat again because the bone was gone. The crane had no reward to carry away, only the memory of what he had said before and after it helped him.

B1.text:
A wolf swallowed food too quickly, and a bone became stuck in his throat. He could not reach it with his paws, and it hurt him. The other animals were afraid to help because the wolf had dangerous teeth. He asked a crane, whose long beak could reach into his mouth, to remove the bone. The wolf promised a reward.

The crane hesitated. It understood the danger but decided to help. It carefully placed its beak in the wolf’s mouth and pulled out the bone. The wolf could breathe and eat normally again. The crane then asked for the payment he had promised. The crane stands beyond the wolf’s teeth and looks at the narrow space it must reach. It moves its long beak carefully, trying not to touch the jaws. When it catches the bone, it pulls back little by little. The wolf can breathe again, but the crane steps away before asking for its promised reward.

When the bone came out, the crane withdrew its beak carefully and moved beyond the wolf’s jaws. The wolf could breathe and swallow again. The crane asked for the payment they had agreed on before it put its head in danger. Instead of reaching for a reward, the wolf showed his teeth. He said that allowing the crane to escape alive was payment enough. The bird had no safe way to make him keep his promise. It had entered his mouth to remove the bone, but it would not put its head there a second time to demand fairness. The crane stepped away and left him with the bone on the ground. The wolf went back to his food, no longer in pain. The crane walked off without the reward it had been offered, remembering the difference between his words before the rescue and his words afterward.

The animals feared his big teeth. A Crane had a long beak and neck. The Wolf asked her to get the bone. The bone hurt each time the Wolf ate.

He said he would give her a gift. The Crane put her beak inside his mouth. She pulled out the bone and stepped back.

Now the Wolf could eat again. The Crane asked for her gift. The Wolf showed her his sharp teeth. The Crane had done just what he asked.

He said she should be glad to be safe. He gave her nothing at all. The Crane walked away from the Wolf.

title: The Old Buccaneer: Chapters I–VI
originalTitles: I. The Old Sea-dog at the Admiral Benbow
II. Black Dog Appears and Disappears
V. The Last of the Blind Man
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Jim Hawkins lives with his parents at the Admiral Benbow inn beside the sea. An old sailor called Billy Bones arrives carrying a locked chest. He pays Jim to watch for a one-legged seaman and spends many hours looking toward the road and the water. At night he drinks, sings frightening songs, and tells stories that make the guests leave. Dr. Livesey visits the inn and warns Billy that his drinking will harm him. When Black Dog, another sailor, arrives, the men argue and draw their swords. Billy collapses after the fight, and the doctor treats him.

Jim's father dies, and Jim and his mother must manage the inn while Billy grows weaker. A blind pirate named Pew comes with a black spot, a warning that Billy's old shipmates want his papers. Billy dies soon afterward. Jim and his mother know the pirates may return. They open his chest to collect the money he owes them while the road outside grows noisy. Jim holds the candle while his mother looks through the chest. She counts only the coins owed to the inn, although he can hear Pew’s cane tapping outside. Beneath the clothes Jim finds an oilskin packet. He takes it as the pirates reach the door, and the two slip into the dark. From their hiding place Jim hears the men overturn furniture inside the inn.

The pirates search the chest, but the packet is gone. Riders arrive, and the pirates scatter; Pew falls beneath a horse in the confusion. Jim takes the packet to Livesey and Squire Trelawney. They open it and find Flint's map showing the island where the old pirate buried his treasure. Trelawney begins planning a voyage to the island. Jim has escaped the men who wanted the map, yet the papers now place him at the start of another dangerous journey.

B2.text:
Jim Hawkins lives with his parents at the Admiral Benbow inn beside the sea. An old sailor called Billy Bones arrives carrying a locked chest. He pays Jim to watch for a one-legged seaman and spends many hours looking toward the road and the water. At night he drinks, sings frightening songs, and tells stories that make the guests leave. Dr. Livesey visits the inn and warns Billy that his drinking will harm him. When Black Dog, another sailor, arrives, the men argue and draw their swords. Billy collapses after the fight, and the doctor treats him. Billy often asks whether Jim has seen the one-legged man, but he says little about why he fears him. His locked chest and sudden anger make the inn feel less safe to the boy who works there.

Jim's father dies, and Jim and his mother must manage the inn while Billy grows weaker. A blind pirate named Pew comes with a black spot, a warning that Billy's old shipmates want his papers. Billy dies soon afterward. Jim and his mother know the pirates may return. They open his chest to collect the money he owes them while the road outside grows noisy. Jim holds the candle while his mother looks through the chest. She counts only the coins owed to the inn, although he can hear Pew’s cane tapping outside. Beneath the clothes Jim finds an oilskin packet. He takes it as the pirates reach the door, and the two slip into the dark. From their hiding place Jim hears the men overturn furniture inside the inn. Pew presses the black spot into Billy’s hand and leaves him with a deadline. Billy’s sudden death gives Jim no chance to ask what the mark means. His mother insists on an honest account of the money even when she hears footsteps outside.

The pirates search the chest, but the packet is gone. Riders arrive, and the pirates scatter; Pew falls beneath a horse in the confusion. Jim takes the packet to Livesey and Squire Trelawney. They open it and find Flint's map showing the island where the old pirate buried his treasure. Trelawney begins planning a voyage to the island. Jim has escaped the men who wanted the map, yet the papers now place him at the start of another dangerous journey. The map has marks that the doctor and squire study closely. Trelawney can supply a ship and crew, while Livesey knows that the men from the inn may still be hunting for the same packet. Jim listens as their plan takes shape.

title: The Sea-cook: Chapters VII–XII
originalTitles: VIII. At the Sign of the Spy-glass
XI. What I Heard in the Apple-Barrel
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Squire Trelawney buys the Hispaniola and hires a crew for the voyage. Jim travels to Bristol and meets the ship's cook, Long John Silver. Silver has one leg, like the man Billy Bones feared, but his friendly manner wins Jim's trust. Captain Smollett is less comfortable with the preparations. He learns that sailors know where the ship is going even though the purpose was meant to be secret. He asks Trelawney to move the weapons and powder close to the loyal passengers. The squire dislikes the warning, but Dr. Livesey supports the captain. At Bristol Jim sees the new ship in the harbour and visits Silver at the Spy-glass tavern. Black Dog is there but runs away when Jim recognizes him. Silver sends men after the visitor and acts surprised that a pirate would enter his place. Jim reports what he saw, while Silver continues to speak warmly to the passengers.

The Hispaniola sails toward the island. Silver works hard in the galley and speaks kindly to Jim. The boy watches him organize the crew and begins to forget his first worry about the missing leg. Smollett remains careful while the ship crosses the sea. One evening Jim climbs into an apple barrel to take the last fruit. Before he can leave, Silver and other sailors gather nearby. Jim stays hidden and listens.

Silver tells the men that he once served under Captain Flint. He has persuaded many of the crew to join him, but he wants them to wait until the honest passengers have found the treasure. Then the pirates will seize it. Jim hears how Silver calms a sailor who wants to act sooner. After the men move away, Jim leaves the barrel and tells Livesey, Trelawney, and Smollett what he heard. They can no longer trust most of their crew. The island is close, and they must decide whom they can rely on before anyone knows that Jim heard the plan.

The long crossing gives him time to hold his followers together.

Silver tells the men that he once served under Captain Flint. He has persuaded many of the crew to join him, but he wants them to wait until the honest passengers have found the treasure. Then the pirates will seize it. Jim hears how Silver calms a sailor who wants to act sooner. After the men move away, Jim leaves the barrel and tells Livesey, Trelawney, and Smollett what he heard. They can no longer trust most of their crew. The island is close, and they must decide whom they can rely on before anyone knows that Jim heard the plan. Jim hears the men discuss when to strike and realizes that the cook has been patient for a reason. He cannot move without shaking the barrel. Later the loyal group speaks quietly because warning the pirates too soon would leave them outnumbered.

title: My Shore Adventure and the Stockade: Chapters XIII–XXI
originalTitles: XIII. How I Began My Shore Adventure
XV. The Man of the Island
XVI. How the Ship Was Abandoned
XVIII. End of the First Day’s Fighting
XIX. The Garrison in the Stockade
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
The Hispaniola reaches the island, and Jim goes ashore with some of Silver's men. He slips away among the trees and hears Silver argue with a sailor who refuses to join the mutiny. Silver kills the man. Jim runs through the undergrowth with no weapon and no safe path back to the landing place. A wild-looking stranger steps out before him: Ben Gunn, a former pirate left on the island years earlier. Ben asks whether Dr. Livesey is with Jim and begs for a passage home. He hints that the treasure hunt may surprise the men who have Flint's map.

Meanwhile the doctor, Squire Trelawney, Captain Smollett, and their loyal companions have left the ship for an old stockade. They make several dangerous trips in a small boat, carrying powder, food, and other supplies while pirates watch from shore. The fence gives them a place to defend, and a spring supplies water. Jim rejoins them there and tells the doctor about Ben Gunn. Outside the walls, Silver gathers the mutineers and prepares to demand the map. Ben Gunn says he has been alone for three years. He talks of cheese, food he has missed since the other pirates abandoned him. Jim promises to tell the doctor where to find him. When Jim reaches the stockade, the loyal group has already lost men bringing supplies ashore. They have to guard the fence, tend the wounded, and keep watch for Silver’s next move.

Silver approaches under a flag and offers safety if Smollett surrenders Flint's map. The captain refuses. Silver leaves angrily, and the defenders take positions around the fence. Pirates rush the stockade. Smoke makes it hard to see who is moving between the trees, and shots come from several directions. The loyal group drives the attackers back, but some of their own people are killed or wounded. Jim stays inside with the others, knowing that the pirates still hold much of the island.

B2.text:
The Hispaniola reaches the island, and Jim goes ashore with some of Silver's men. He slips away among the trees and hears Silver argue with a sailor who refuses to join the mutiny. Silver kills the man. Jim runs through the undergrowth with no weapon and no safe path back to the landing place. A wild-looking stranger steps out before him: Ben Gunn, a former pirate left on the island years earlier. Ben asks whether Dr. Livesey is with Jim and begs for a passage home. He hints that the treasure hunt may surprise the men who have Flint's map. Jim hears the loyal sailor refuse Silver and then hears the cry that follows. He has seen enough to know that Silver will kill anyone who stands in the mutineers’ way. Ben Gunn speaks quickly after years with almost no company.

Meanwhile the doctor, Squire Trelawney, Captain Smollett, and their loyal companions have left the ship for an old stockade. They make several dangerous trips in a small boat, carrying powder, food, and other supplies while pirates watch from shore. The fence gives them a place to defend, and a spring supplies water. Jim rejoins them there and tells the doctor about Ben Gunn. Outside the walls, Silver gathers the mutineers and prepares to demand the map. Ben Gunn says he has been alone for three years. He talks of cheese, food he has missed since the other pirates abandoned him. Jim promises to tell the doctor where to find him. When Jim reaches the stockade, the loyal group has already lost men bringing supplies ashore. They have to guard the fence, tend the wounded, and keep watch for Silver’s next move. The doctor’s party has to move its supplies before the pirates control the shore. The small boat sits low in the water as they carry the last load. They choose the stockade because its fence and spring offer a chance to hold out.

Silver approaches under a flag and offers safety if Smollett surrenders Flint's map. The captain refuses; Silver leaves angrily, and the defenders take positions around the fence. Pirates rush the stockade. Smoke makes it hard to see who is moving between the trees, and shots come from several directions. The loyal group drives the attackers back, but some of their own people are killed or wounded. Jim stays inside with the others, knowing that the pirates still hold much of the island. The men inside the fence wait until the attackers come close. After the fight they count the people who can still defend the walls and care for the wounded. Their victory gives them shelter, but it does not give them the ship.

title: Captain Silver: Chapters XXII–XXXIV
originalTitles: XXII. How I Began My Sea Adventure
XXIV. The Cruise of the Coracle
XXV. I Strike the Jolly Roger
XXXII. The Treasure-hunt—The Voice Among the Trees
XXXIII. The Fall of a Chieftain
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Jim leaves the stockade and finds Ben Gunn's little boat. At night he paddles toward the Hispaniola and cuts its anchor rope. The current pulls the ship away from the pirates. After a dangerous trip in the small craft, Jim climbs aboard the drifting vessel. Israel Hands is wounded but promises to help him steer. Jim guides the ship toward a quiet inlet, watching Hands carefully. When Hands attacks, Jim climbs into the rigging and fires at him. Hands falls into the water. Jim has saved the ship, but the loyal party does not yet know where he is. Jim uses Ben Gunn’s small boat at night, fighting the current as he reaches the Hispaniola. He cuts the anchor rope and lets the tide carry the ship away from the pirates’ landing place. When he climbs aboard later, he finds one sailor dead and Hands injured. Hands helps steer for a while, then reaches for a weapon.

He returns to the stockade in the dark and discovers that Silver's men now occupy it. They capture Jim, and some want to kill him. Silver stops them, hoping to use the boy in a bargain with Livesey. The pirates challenge Silver's leadership and give him a black spot, but he shows them Flint's map and persuades them to follow him. The doctor visits Jim and asks him to escape. Jim refuses because he has promised Silver not to run. Livesey leaves with that promise still in place.

Silver leads the pirates and Jim to the place marked on the map. They find an empty pit. The gold has already been moved by Ben Gunn. The angry men turn on Silver, but Livesey and the loyal group arrive and drive them off. Jim learns how Ben hid the treasure after his years alone on the island. The survivors carry it to the ship and sail away. Silver slips away at a port on the return voyage. Jim reaches home with a share of the gold, though he does not wish to go back to that island.

He cuts the anchor rope and lets the tide carry the ship away from the pirates’ landing place. When he climbs aboard later, he finds one sailor dead and Hands injured. Hands helps steer for a while, then reaches for a weapon.

He returns to the stockade in the dark and discovers that Silver's men now occupy it. They capture Jim, and some want to kill him. Silver stops them, hoping to use the boy in a bargain with Livesey. The pirates challenge Silver's leadership and give him a black spot, but he shows them Flint's map and persuades them to follow him. The doctor visits Jim and asks him to escape. Jim refuses because he has promised Silver not to run. Livesey leaves with that promise still in place.

Silver leads the pirates and Jim to the place marked on the map. They find an empty pit. The gold has already been moved by Ben Gunn. The angry men turn on Silver, but Livesey and the loyal group arrive and drive them off. Jim learns how Ben hid the treasure after his years alone on the island. The survivors carry it to the ship and sail away. Silver slips away at a port on the return voyage. Jim reaches home with a share of the gold, though he does not wish to go back to that island.

title: The Time Machine: The Time Traveller and His Machine
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
The Time Traveller invites guests to dinner and asks them to imagine time as another direction through which a person might move. They doubt him. He sets a small model on a table and asks a guest to touch its lever. The model vanishes. Some guests search beneath the table while others suspect a trick. The inventor tells them that a larger machine waits in his workshop. When they gather again a week later, he is late. He appears with torn clothes and dirt on his face, eats, and begins to describe the journey he has just made.

He sat on the large machine and pressed its controls. Day and night flashed past as years rushed around him. Buildings changed and vanished. He stopped in the distant year 802,701 and fell beside the machine. The world around him was warm and green. Small people called the Eloi came to meet him. They offered fruit and led him into a great building. He tried to learn their words and ask how they lived, but they quickly tired of his questions. Their easy life made him think at first that future people faced no work or danger. The traveller puts the control levers in his pocket before walking away from the machine. From a hill he can see the strange white figure and the great hall where the Eloi gather. They serve him fruit, then drift away from his questions. He returns to the machine before night, expecting to find it where he left it.

The traveller returned to the place where he had left his machine. It was gone. Marks in the grass showed that something heavy had been moved, though he had kept the control levers with him. Nearby stood a white stone figure with closed bronze doors beneath it. He searched the ground and tried to question the Eloi, but they gave him no clear answer. Without the machine he could not return to his own time. He had arrived ready to explore; now he had to find what someone had taken.
shortSummary: The Time Traveller explains that time is a dimension like length or height. His guests doubt him, so he shows them a small machine that can move through time.

He returns to the machine before night, expecting to find it where he left it. As the years race past, the sun seems to rise and set faster and faster. The traveller stops the machine suddenly and looks around at unfamiliar plants and buildings. He keeps the levers in his pocket before walking toward the people.

The traveller returned to the place where he had left his machine; it was gone. Marks in the grass showed that something heavy had been moved, though he had kept the control levers with him. Without the machine he could not return to his own time. He had arrived ready to explore; now he had to find what someone had taken. The stone figure is large enough to hide an entrance. The traveller sees no way through its bronze doors. He cannot yet tell whether the Eloi moved the machine or whether another group shares their world.

title: The Time Machine: The Eloi and the Missing Machine
originalTitles: III. The Time Traveller Returns; IV. Time Travelling
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
The Time Traveller lives among the Eloi while he searches for his missing machine. They offer him food and shelter, but they cannot explain where the device has gone. One day he sees a young Eloi carried away by water while others keep playing. He jumps in and brings her to shore. Her name is Weena. She follows him afterward and gives him flowers. The friendship helps him learn more about the people around him, although their language remains hard for him to understand.

Near the white stone figure, the traveller finds marks in the grass where the machine stood. He knows it cannot have travelled away through time because he kept its levers. The bronze doors below the figure are shut. He feels around their edges and asks the Eloi about them, but they avoid the question. Weena becomes frightened as the light fades. Other Eloi gather together rather than stay alone. Their beautiful halls feel less safe at night than they did by day. The traveller spends daylight circling the stone figure and studying the grass. He points to the bronze doors, hoping the Eloi will explain them, but they move away or laugh. Weena stays near him after he has helped her. Her fear when evening comes makes his search for the missing machine more urgent.

The traveller notices a pale figure moving among the bushes. It disappears down a well. He goes closer and feels air coming from below; he can hear distant machinery too. The Eloi live above ground, enjoying fruit and sunlight, but another kind of person may be working underneath them. He thinks again of the closed doors beneath the stone figure. B2.text:
The Time Traveller lives among the Eloi while he searches for his missing machine. They offer him food and shelter, but they cannot explain where the device has gone. One day he sees a young Eloi carried away by water while others keep playing. He jumps in and brings her to shore; her name is Weena. She follows him afterward and gives him flowers. The friendship helps him learn more about the people around him, although their language remains hard for him to understand. The Eloi who watched Weena fall into the water did not try to rescue her. The traveller is surprised by their indifference. Weena’s gratitude gives him a companion in a world where he understands almost no one.

Near the white stone figure, the traveller finds marks in the grass where the machine stood. He knows it cannot have travelled away through time because he kept its levers. The bronze doors below the figure are shut. He feels around their edges and asks the Eloi about them, but they avoid the question. Weena becomes frightened as the light fades; other Eloi gather together rather than stay alone. Their beautiful halls feel less safe at night than they did by day. The traveller spends daylight circling the stone figure and studying the grass. He points to the bronze doors, hoping the Eloi will explain them, but they move away or laugh. Weena stays near him after he has helped her. Her fear when evening comes makes his search for the missing machine more urgent. Narrow tracks lead across the grass toward the stone structure. The traveller tests the doors but cannot shift them. His own missing levers remain in his pocket, proof that the machine itself is still somewhere nearby.

The traveller notices a pale figure moving among the bushes. It disappears down a well. He goes closer and feels air coming from below; he can hear distant machinery too. The Eloi live above ground, enjoying fruit and sunlight, but another kind of person may be working underneath them. He thinks again of the closed doors beneath the stone figure. As darkness grows, Weena stays beside him. He has found signs of people who might know where his machine is, but he does not yet know whether they will help him. At the well the air moves steadily upward, as if machines are working below. A pale face appears for a moment and vanishes. The traveller begins to understand why the Eloi avoid dark places and why their answers have been so thin.

title: The Time Machine: The Morlocks Below
originalTitles: V. In the Golden Age; VI. The Sunset of Mankind; VII. A Sudden Shock; VIII. Explanation
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
The traveller climbs down a well after seeing a pale figure vanish into it. Deep below the ground he finds the Morlocks. Their large eyes suit the darkness, and machines run around their workrooms. He first thinks they may serve the Eloi above, but their hands reach toward him and he has to escape. Back in the sunlight, he tells Weena little of what he saw. Her fear of the dark now makes sense. He is certain that the people below can come up at night, and he still has no machine with which to leave.

The traveller and Weena set out for the Palace of Green Porcelain, a distant building above the valley. It was once a museum, but its displays are broken and dust covers the rooms. He searches for anything that might protect them. He finds a metal bar, matches, and camphor. Fire makes the Morlocks retreat, so the matches are especially valuable. Weena walks close to him as they leave the Palace. Their journey back is long, and daylight is fading before they reach the place where the machine disappeared. He enters the Palace with Weena and looks through dusty rooms that once held exhibits. A metal bar may serve as a weapon, while the matches and camphor will help him make light. They cannot stay there forever. The long walk back toward the stone figure will take them across open land and a wood.

They enter a wood at dusk. The trees hide the last light, and Weena is tired from walking. The traveller gathers sticks and starts a fire. He puts the metal bar within reach and checks how many matches remain. Pale shapes move beyond the flames. He wants to lead Weena out of the wood before the fire dies, but the Morlocks are already near. For the moment the light keeps them back, and the two travellers wait together beside it.

He looks through cabinets and broken displays for things he can carry. Weena watches him gather what they will need after sunset.

title: The Time Machine: Beyond the Human Future
originalTitles: IX. The Morlocks; X. When Night Came; XI. The Palace of Green Porcelain; XII. The Further Vision; XIII. The Trap in the White Sphinx; XIV. The Further Vision
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
A fire spreads through the wood while the traveller tries to keep the Morlocks away from Weena. Smoke covers the trees, and he loses her in the confusion. When morning comes, he searches among the burned branches but cannot find her. The Morlocks have fled the flames. Grieving and alone, he returns toward the white stone figure where his machine disappeared. The bronze doors beneath it now stand open. Inside he sees the machine, but the doors close behind him and the Morlocks rush in. The travellers have crossed the wood together, so Weena’s disappearance leaves the Time Traveller searching through smoke for the person who trusted him. He cannot find her. The rising heat drives the Morlocks away, but it gives him no answer about where she went. He goes on toward the white stone figure alone.

He reaches the machine and fits its control levers as the pale figures close around him. The floor seems to vanish when he starts it. He travels farther into the future and stops beside a cold sea. A huge crab-like creature moves on the shore under a dim red sun. He goes still farther and sees a world with almost no life. The lonely sight sends him back toward the time he knows. He reverses the machine and returns to his own workshop.

At dinner the Time Traveller tells his guests what happened. Some question his account, while the narrator listens and looks at the strange flowers Weena gave him. The traveller has brought those flowers and his damaged clothes back from the future, but they cannot show the others every part of the journey. The next day the narrator visits again. He sees the Time Traveller leave with the machine for another trip. He waits for him to return, yet the inventor does not come back.

A fire spreads through the wood while the traveller tries to keep the Morlocks away from Weena. Smoke covers the trees, and he loses her in the confusion. When morning comes, he searches among the burned branches but cannot find her. The Morlocks have fled the flames. Grieving and alone, he returns toward the white stone figure where his machine disappeared. The bronze doors beneath it now stand open. Inside he sees the machine, but the doors close behind him and the Morlocks rush in. The travellers have crossed the wood together, so Weena’s disappearance leaves the Time Traveller searching through smoke for the person who trusted him. He cannot find her. The rising heat drives the Morlocks away, but it gives him no answer about where she went. He goes on toward the white stone figure alone.

He reaches the machine and fits its control levers as the pale figures close around him. The floor seems to vanish when he starts it. He travels farther into the future and stops beside a cold sea. A huge crab-like creature moves on the shore under a dim red sun. He goes still farther and sees a world with almost no life. The lonely sight sends him back toward the time he knows. He reverses the machine and returns to his own workshop.

At dinner the Time Traveller tells his guests what happened. Some question his account, while the narrator listens and looks at the strange flowers Weena gave him. The traveller has brought those flowers and his damaged clothes back from the future, but they cannot show the others every part of the journey. The next day the narrator visits again. title: Frankenstein: A Dangerous Ambition
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Robert Walton writes to his sister from a ship sailing into Arctic ice. He hopes to find a northern passage and make a great discovery. One day the crew sees a huge figure travelling over the frozen sea. The next day they rescue a weaker traveller whose sled has broken down. The man is Victor Frankenstein. He asks where the ship is going, and Walton tells him about his plans. Victor hears the explorer's hunger for discovery and says that his own story may serve as a warning.

Victor begins with his childhood in Geneva. Elizabeth grows up in his family, and Henry Clerval is his close friend. At university Victor studies the natural world and becomes determined to discover how life begins. At Ingolstadt, Victor first meets teachers who challenge his old reading. He attends lectures and learns new ways to study chemistry. Their work makes him think he can reach a secret that others have missed. The longer he works, the less he writes to Elizabeth and his father. He keeps his door shut while his friends wonder why he has disappeared from their lives. He works alone for months, bringing materials to his room and ignoring letters from home. He forgets the seasons outside while he builds a body. Victor imagines that the new being will thank him, but he has not prepared for the moment when it opens its eyes.

On a rainy night his experiment succeeds. The creature moves, and its appearance terrifies Victor. He leaves the room and tries to sleep, but wakes from a frightening dream to find the creature standing beside his bed. It reaches toward him. Victor runs away again and wanders through the streets until morning. There he meets Henry, who has just arrived to study. Henry expects to find his friend at work, but Victor can scarcely speak about the laboratory. Henry looks after him through a long illness. When Victor eventually returns to his room, the creature is gone. He has no idea where it went or what will happen to it.

At university Victor studies the natural world and becomes determined to discover how life begins. At Ingolstadt, Victor first meets teachers who challenge his old reading. He attends lectures and learns new ways to study chemistry. Their work makes him think he can reach a secret that others have missed. The longer he works, the less he writes to Elizabeth and his father. He keeps his door shut while his friends wonder why he has disappeared from their lives. He works alone for months, bringing materials to his room and ignoring letters from home. He forgets the seasons outside while he builds a body. Victor imagines that the new being will thank him, but he has not prepared for the moment when it opens its eyes. Victor visits places connected with death to learn how bodies are made. His work keeps him away from the people who care for him. He believes success is near and refuses to pause for rest.

On a rainy night his experiment succeeds; the creature moves, and its appearance terrifies Victor. He leaves the room and tries to sleep, but wakes from a frightening dream to find the creature standing beside his bed. It reaches toward him; Victor runs away again and wanders through the streets until morning. There he meets Henry, who has just arrived to study. Henry expects to find his friend at work, but Victor can scarcely speak about the laboratory. Henry looks after him through a long illness; when Victor eventually returns to his room, the creature is gone. He has no idea where it went or what will happen to it. Henry sees Victor shaking and feverish but cannot learn why. Victor cannot bring himself to describe the being he left behind. He lets Henry care for him while keeping the secret that caused his collapse.

title: Frankenstein: The Creature Learns Alone
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Victor recovers from the illness that followed his experiment. Henry Clerval cares for him, and the creature he brought to life is gone from the room where he left it. Victor avoids speaking about it. A letter from home tells him that his youngest brother William has been murdered near Geneva. He travels back, shocked by the loss. title: Frankenstein: A Request and a Refusal
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Victor travels into the mountains after the deaths in his family. On a glacier the creature he made approaches him. Victor wants to attack, but the creature asks him to listen first. It leads Victor to a shelter and describes waking alone, hungry, and cold. People fled when they saw its face. It hid near a cottage and learned language by watching the family who lived there. It helped them secretly by bringing wood. When it finally tried to speak with the blind father, the other family members returned and drove it away.

The creature tells Victor that loneliness has made its life unbearable. It asks him to create a companion like itself. If Victor agrees, the two beings will leave people and live far away. Victor fears what might happen if he refuses, but he also fears making another creature. He begins the work in a lonely place, keeping it secret from his family. As the second body takes shape, he imagines that it might reject the first or that they might harm others together. The creature watched a family from a hidden shelter. It learned words as the people spoke to one another and saw how they shared food, work, and affection. When it finally entered their home, the blind father listened kindly, but the others returned and drove it away. That rejection shaped the request it now brings to Victor.

The first creature comes to watch him. Victor tears apart the unfinished companion before he can bring it to life. The creature sees what he has done and vows to be with him on his wedding night. Victor clears away the pieces and takes them onto the water, but the threat follows him. He has refused the request; now he must return to people he loves while knowing that the being he made has promised revenge.
shortSummary: Victor leaves home and travels alone, hoping that mountains and open air will calm him. On a glacier, the creature finds him and asks him to listen.

B2.text:

It leads Victor to a shelter and describes waking alone, hungry, and cold. People fled when they saw its face. It hid near a cottage and learned language by watching the family who lived there. The creature recalls the first fires it found and the food it learned to seek. Every attempt to approach people ended with fear or blows. It wants Victor to hear these events before judging it.

The creature tells Victor that loneliness has made its life unbearable. It asks him to create a companion like itself. If Victor agrees, the two beings will leave people and live far away. It learned words as the people spoke to one another and saw how they shared food, work, and affection. When it finally entered their home, the blind father listened kindly, but the others returned and drove it away. That rejection shaped the request it now brings to Victor. In the cottage, it had watched the family teach a visitor new words. By listening through a crack in the wall, it learned to tell Victor what happened. Its request for company comes from those months of watching other people live together.

The first creature comes to watch him. Victor tears apart the unfinished companion before he can bring it to life. The creature sees what he has done and vows to be with him on his wedding night. Victor clears away the pieces and takes them onto the water, but the threat follows him. He has refused the request; now he must return to people he loves while knowing that the being he made has promised revenge. Victor’s hands stop over the unfinished body when he sees the creature outside. Destroying it ends the work but not the danger. The visitor’s promise sends him back across the water with a fear he cannot share openly.

title: Frankenstein: The Pursuit into the Ice
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Victor returns to his family while the creature's threat hangs over him. His friend Henry Clerval is killed, and Victor is accused when the body is found. He is eventually cleared, but he goes home exhausted. He marries Elizabeth, hoping to protect her on the night the creature promised to come. Victor watches for an attack on himself. Then he hears Elizabeth cry out and finds her dead. His father dies soon afterward. Victor has now lost nearly everyone close to him. Victor believes the wedding-night threat is aimed at him. He watches doors and paths for an attack while Elizabeth waits for him. A cry from her room shows that he misunderstood. After losing her, he tells an official of the creature and begs for help, but the chase soon takes him beyond the places where others can follow.

He follows the creature across towns, mountains, and frozen land. The creature leaves signs that keep Victor on its trail, sometimes giving him just enough food to continue. Victor asks others for help, but the chase reaches places where they cannot follow for long. His strength begins to fail on the ice. Robert Walton's ship finds him and brings him aboard. Walton listens as Victor finishes the account he began after his rescue. Victor urges him to think about his crew's safety instead of risking their lives for his own ambition.

The sailors want to leave the ice and return home. Walton agrees. Victor dies before the ship can escape. Later Walton sees the creature beside Victor's body. It mourns the man it hated and the suffering it has caused. It says it will go away and end its own life, then disappears over the ice. Walton watches it leave. He cannot bring Victor back or follow the creature; he can only turn his ship toward home with the story he has heard.
shortSummary: Victor returns to his family, but the creature’s threat follows him. Henry Clerval is killed, and Victor is accused before he can prove where he was.

B1.text:
Victor returns to his family while the creature's threat hangs over him. His friend Henry Clerval is killed, and Victor is accused when the body is found. He is eventually cleared, but he goes home exhausted. He marries Elizabeth, hoping to protect her on the night the creature promised to come. Victor watches for an attack on himself. Then he hears Elizabeth cry out and finds her dead. His father dies soon afterward. Victor has now lost nearly everyone close to him. Victor believes the wedding-night threat is aimed at him. He watches doors and paths for an attack while Elizabeth waits for him. A cry from her room shows that he misunderstood. After losing her, he tells an official of the creature and begs for help, but the chase soon takes him beyond the places where others can follow.

He follows the creature across towns, mountains, and frozen land. The creature leaves signs that keep Victor on its trail, sometimes giving him just enough food to continue. Victor asks others for help, but the chase reaches places where they cannot follow for long. His strength begins to fail on the ice. Robert Walton's ship finds him and brings him aboard. Walton listens as Victor finishes the account he began after his rescue. Victor urges him to think about his crew's safety instead of risking their lives for his own ambition.

The sailors want to leave the ice and return home. Walton agrees. Victor dies before the ship can escape. Later Walton sees the creature beside Victor's body. It mourns the man it hated and the suffering it has caused. It says it will go away and end its own life, then disappears over the ice. Walton watches it leave. He cannot bring Victor back or follow the creature; he can only turn his ship toward home with the story he has heard.

B2.text:
Victor returns to his family while the creature's threat hangs over him. His friend Henry Clerval is killed, and Victor is accused when the body is found. He is eventually cleared, but he goes home exhausted. He marries Elizabeth, hoping to protect her on the night the creature promised to come. Victor watches for an attack on himself; then he hears Elizabeth cry out and finds her dead. His father dies soon afterward; Victor has now lost nearly everyone close to him. Victor believes the wedding-night threat is aimed at him. He watches doors and paths for an attack while Elizabeth waits for him. A cry from her room shows that he misunderstood. After losing her, he tells an official of the creature and begs for help, but the chase soon takes him beyond the places where others can follow. After Henry’s death, Victor has to answer questions about a crime he did not commit. He survives the accusation, but his secret remains with him when he returns to Elizabeth. He keeps watch at the wrong door.

He follows the creature across towns, mountains, and frozen land. The creature leaves signs that keep Victor on its trail, sometimes giving him just enough food to continue. Victor asks others for help, but the chase reaches places where they cannot follow for long. His strength begins to fail on the ice; robert Walton's ship finds him and brings him aboard. Walton listens as Victor finishes the account he began after his rescue. Victor urges him to think about his crew's safety instead of risking their lives for his own ambition. The creature’s trail leads through cold places where Victor can barely find food or rest. Walton’s sailors first see another large figure on the ice, then find Victor weakened on a sled. The explorer’s ship becomes the last place Victor tells his story.

The sailors want to leave the ice and return home. Walton agrees; Victor dies before the ship can escape. Later Walton sees the creature beside Victor's body. It mourns the man it hated and the suffering it has caused. It says it will go away and end its own life, then disappears over the ice. Walton watches it leave. He cannot bring Victor back or follow the creature; he can only turn his ship toward home with the story he has heard. The creature speaks to Walton without asking for forgiveness. It says that revenge has left it alone with the deaths it caused. Walton hears the words, then sees the figure move away across the frozen sea.

title: The Call of the Wild: Buck Is Taken North
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Buck is a strong dog living with Judge Miller's family in California. He knows the paths around their ranch and expects food, warmth, and gentle voices. During the northern gold rush, a gardener's helper secretly sells him. Buck is tied, put into a crate, and passed from one stranger to another. He fights against the men who hold him, but he cannot return to the ranch. At one stop, a man in a red sweater strikes him with a club each time he charges. Buck learns that he cannot win that fight by strength alone. On Judge Miller’s ranch Buck walked among the family and slept in a warm place. The gardener’s helper takes him away when men are paying for large dogs in the North. Buck struggles against the rope and the crate, but each train and ship carries him farther from home. No familiar person comes to bring him back.

Buck travels north with other dogs. The air grows colder, and the ground is covered with snow. He watches a dog named Curly greet another animal, only to be attacked and killed by a group. The sudden violence teaches Buck to keep his distance when dogs are fighting. He has never had to search for a safe place to sleep or defend his food before. Now he watches the older dogs closely and learns where to curl beneath the snow for warmth.

Men put Buck into a harness with a sled team. He does not know the commands, so the dogs and drivers show him when to pull, stop, and turn. The work is hard, and a mistake can slow the whole team. Buck watches the leader Spitz, who is quick and experienced but ready to threaten a weaker dog. Each day Buck understands a little more of the new rules. He has not forgotten his old home, yet he must learn the northern trail if he is to survive there.

B2.text:
Buck is a strong dog living with Judge Miller's family in California. He knows the paths around their ranch and expects food, warmth, and gentle voices. During the northern gold rush, a gardener's helper secretly sells him. Buck is tied, put into a crate, and passed from one stranger to another. He fights against the men who hold him, but he cannot return to the ranch. At one stop, a man in a red sweater strikes him with a club each time he charges. Buck learns that he cannot win that fight by strength alone. On Judge Miller’s ranch Buck walked among the family and slept in a warm place. The gardener’s helper takes him away when men are paying for large dogs in the North. Buck struggles against the rope and the crate, but each train and ship carries him farther from home. No familiar person comes to bring him back. Buck had been treated almost like a member of the household. The sale changes his life in a single afternoon, but the journey north takes many stages. At each one he waits for someone he knows to appear.

Buck travels north with other dogs. The air grows colder, and the ground is covered with snow. He watches a dog named Curly greet another animal, only to be attacked and killed by a group. The sudden violence teaches Buck to keep his distance when dogs are fighting. He has never had to search for a safe place to sleep or defend his food before. Now he watches the older dogs closely and learns where to curl beneath the snow for warmth. The man with the club does not need to chase Buck; he waits until the dog attacks and then strikes. Buck learns to stand back, though he does not come to like the man. Curly’s death shows him another danger that no human will explain.

Men put Buck into a harness with a sled team. He does not know the commands, so the dogs and drivers show him when to pull, stop, and turn. The work is hard, and a mistake can slow the whole team. Buck watches the leader Spitz, who is quick and experienced but ready to threaten a weaker dog. Each day Buck understands a little more of the new rules. He has not forgotten his old home, yet he must learn the northern trail if he is to survive there. The leather traces connect Buck’s effort to the heavy sled. He feels the pull when the team starts and the strain when one dog falls behind. Watching Spitz teaches him as much as the drivers’ shouted commands.

title: The Call of the Wild: The Team and the Trail
originalTitles: II. The Law of Club and Fang; III. The Dominant Primordial Beast
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Buck pulls a sled across the northern trail with Spitz and the other dogs. The team travels long distances in cold weather and stops wherever the drivers can make camp. Buck learns to curl under the snow for warmth and to take food before another dog can steal it. He listens for commands and watches how each dog keeps the sled moving. Spitz leads the team, but he uses his experience to threaten Buck. The two dogs challenge each other more often as Buck becomes stronger. At one camp Buck digs a hole in the snow to sleep. Spitz takes the place before Buck can settle in it. Buck bares his teeth, and the dogs circle each other until another sound draws them away. The quarrel stays with them when they are harnessed for the next day’s run.

One night a rabbit runs from the camp. Buck and Spitz chase it across the snow. Buck nearly reaches the animal, but Spitz cuts across his path. The two dogs turn toward each other and fight away from the team. Spitz is used to winning, yet Buck changes the way he attacks. He catches Spitz off balance and brings him down. The other dogs close in on the fallen leader. Buck returns to the sled knowing that the place at its front is now open.

The next morning the drivers try to put another dog in the lead position. Buck refuses to move back. He avoids their hands and stands where Spitz stood. After several attempts they let him take the place. Buck responds quickly when the path bends and keeps the other dogs pulling together. The team makes better time under him. He has won a fight, but he must also show that he can guide the team through each day's work.
shortSummary: Buck learns how to steal food without being caught and how to curl in the snow for warmth. He watches the other dogs and understands that a mistake can bring a fight.

B1.text:
Buck pulls a sled across the northern trail with Spitz and the other dogs. The team travels long distances in cold weather and stops wherever the drivers can make camp. Buck learns to curl under the snow for warmth and to take food before another dog can steal it. He listens for commands and watches how each dog keeps the sled moving. Spitz leads the team, but he uses his experience to threaten Buck. The two dogs challenge each other more often as Buck becomes stronger. At one camp Buck digs a hole in the snow to sleep. Spitz takes the place before Buck can settle in it. Buck bares his teeth, and the dogs circle each other until another sound draws them away. The quarrel stays with them when they are harnessed for the next day’s run.

One night a rabbit runs from the camp. Buck and Spitz chase it across the snow. Buck nearly reaches the animal, but Spitz cuts across his path. The two dogs turn toward each other and fight away from the team. Spitz is used to winning, yet Buck changes the way he attacks. He catches Spitz off balance and brings him down. The other dogs close in on the fallen leader. Buck returns to the sled knowing that the place at its front is now open.

The next morning the drivers try to put another dog in the lead position. Buck refuses to move back. He avoids their hands and stands where Spitz stood. After several attempts they let him take the place. Buck responds quickly when the path bends and keeps the other dogs pulling together. The team makes better time under him. He has won a fight, but he must also show that he can guide the team through each day's work.

B2.text:
Buck pulls a sled across the northern trail with Spitz and the other dogs. The team travels long distances in cold weather and stops wherever the drivers can make camp. Buck learns to curl under the snow for warmth and to take food before another dog can steal it. He listens for commands and watches how each dog keeps the sled moving. Spitz leads the team, but he uses his experience to threaten Buck. The two dogs challenge each other more often as Buck becomes stronger. At one camp Buck digs a hole in the snow to sleep. Spitz takes the place before Buck can settle in it. Buck bares his teeth, and the dogs circle each other until another sound draws them away. The quarrel stays with them when they are harnessed for the next day’s run. The dogs’ traces pull tight when the sled starts, and every delay is felt by the others. Buck learns to read the ground ahead and to move before the drivers have to shout. His skill makes Spitz watch him more closely.

One night a rabbit runs from the camp; Buck and Spitz chase it across the snow. Buck nearly reaches the animal, but Spitz cuts across his path. The two dogs turn toward each other and fight away from the team. Spitz is used to winning, yet Buck changes the way he attacks. He catches Spitz off balance and brings him down. The other dogs close in on the fallen leader. Buck returns to the sled knowing that the place at its front is now open. The chase draws them away from the camp. Buck cannot beat Spitz by rushing straight at him, so he changes direction and catches his rival’s legs. When the fight ends, the pack moves toward the fallen leader.

The next morning the drivers try to put another dog in the lead position. Buck refuses to move back; he avoids their hands and stands where Spitz stood. After several attempts they let him take the place. Buck responds quickly when the path bends and keeps the other dogs pulling together. The team makes better time under him. He has won a fight, but he must also show that he can guide the team through each day's work. Buck circles away whenever the drivers try to place him behind another dog. He returns to the front until they give up. On the trail his quick turns and steady pace show that he wanted more than a prize from the fight.

title: The Call of the Wild: A New Master and a Rescue
originalTitles: IV. Who Has Won to Mastership; V. The Toil of Trace and Trail; VI. For the Love of a Man
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
After Buck becomes leader, the sled team changes hands. Its new owners do not understand the northern trail. They load the sled with too many belongings and fail to plan enough food for the dogs. The team grows weaker each day. Several dogs die, and Buck becomes too thin to pull well. At a river crossing in spring he falls in the traces and cannot rise. The owners shout and prepare to beat him forward, though the ice ahead has begun to break. The new owners pack too much onto the sled and do not carry enough food. They argue about what to leave behind while the dogs stand waiting in the cold. As the journey continues, several animals die and the others weaken. Buck has pulled through hard weather before, but this time his body cannot recover between the long days.

John Thornton sees the exhausted dog and steps between Buck and the people holding the whip. He warns them that the ice will not bear the sled. They refuse to listen. Thornton cuts Buck out of the harness and pulls him away. The rest of the team moves onto the river with its owners. The ice gives way, and they disappear beneath the water. Buck survives because Thornton would not let him take another step.

Thornton feeds Buck and gives him time to recover. Buck follows the man around the camp, sometimes taking his hand gently in his mouth. He has known harsh drivers, but this one treats him with care. As his strength returns, Buck explores the trees beyond camp. He hears distant calls from the forest and stays away a little longer each time. Then he comes back to Thornton. The man who saved him is still waiting there, and Buck has a place beside him.
shortSummary: Buck leads the team after Spitz is gone, but the dogs and sled become exhausted. Their next owners are inexperienced and demand more work than the animals can safely do.

B2.text:
After Buck becomes leader, the sled team changes hands. Its new owners do not understand the northern trail. They load the sled with too many belongings and fail to plan enough food for the dogs. The team grows weaker each day. Several dogs die, and Buck becomes too thin to pull well. At a river crossing in spring he falls in the traces and cannot rise. The owners shout and prepare to beat him forward, though the ice ahead has begun to break. The new owners pack too much onto the sled and do not carry enough food. They argue about what to leave behind while the dogs stand waiting in the cold. As the journey continues, several animals die and the others weaken. Buck has pulled through hard weather before, but this time his body cannot recover between the long days. The owners believe that more shouting will make up for poor planning. Empty food bags and a heavy sled show otherwise. Buck’s legs fail before they reach the river, but they try to force him onward.

John Thornton sees the exhausted dog and steps between Buck and the people holding the whip. He warns them that the ice will not bear the sled; they refuse to listen. Thornton cuts Buck out of the harness and pulls him away. The rest of the team moves onto the river with its owners. The ice gives way, and they disappear beneath the water. Buck survives because Thornton would not let him take another step. Thornton has watched the spring ice and understands how quickly it is breaking. He cuts the straps while the owners protest. The empty place where Buck stood is all that remains of the team after the crossing.

Thornton feeds Buck and gives him time to recover. Buck follows the man around the camp, sometimes taking his hand gently in his mouth. He has known harsh drivers, but this one treats him with care. As his strength returns, Buck explores the trees beyond camp. He hears distant calls from the forest and stays away a little longer each time. Then he comes back to Thornton. The man who saved him is still waiting there, and Buck has a place beside him. Recovery is slow; Buck sleeps and eats before he can roam again. He returns from his first longer walks in the forest to find Thornton at the camp, and that welcome draws him back again.

title: The Call of the Wild: The Wild Answers
originalTitles: VII. The Sounding of the Call
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Buck leaves Thornton's camp for longer journeys into the forest. He hunts and meets a wild wolf. At first the wolf keeps its distance, but they begin to run together. Buck follows it for a time, then returns to the camp where Thornton welcomes him. The calls beyond the trees continue to draw him away. He learns the paths, finds food, and comes back from each journey to the man who saved him. Buck had once slept beside a human fire every night. Now he can spend days alone, finding his way by smell and sound. The wolf he follows waits for him in the trees, then races ahead to show him a trail. Buck turns back to Thornton several times, even when the forest offers food. That choice ends only when the camp is destroyed. After the attack, he pauses by the empty fire and recognizes that Thornton will not call him back again.

One day Buck returns and smells danger before he reaches the tents. The camp has been attacked. He finds Thornton and his companions dead. Men from a nearby group are still there, and Buck charges at them. They scatter, but Buck cannot bring Thornton back. He searches the place where his friend lived and waits for a voice that no longer comes. The fire and tents cannot give him a reason to stay. He goes into the trees and meets the wolf again.

Other wolves approach Buck and test him. He fights when they challenge him, then runs with their pack. His strength and knowledge of the forest help him lead them. The people in the region later speak of a large dog moving among wolves. In summer Buck returns to the place where Thornton died. He stands there for a while, then leaves the old camp and follows the pack into the forest.
shortSummary: Buck leaves camp for longer periods and hunts with a wolf. When he returns, he finds that Thornton and his companions have been killed by men from another group.

Other wolves approach Buck and test him. He fights when they challenge him, then runs with their pack. His strength and knowledge of the forest help him lead them. The people in the region later speak of a large dog moving among wolves. In summer Buck returns to the place where Thornton died. B2.text:
Buck leaves Thornton's camp for longer journeys into the forest; he hunts and meets a wild wolf. At first the wolf keeps its distance, but they begin to run together. Buck follows it for a time, then returns to the camp where Thornton welcomes him. The calls beyond the trees continue to draw him away. He learns the paths, finds food, and comes back from each journey to the man who saved him. Buck had once slept beside a human fire every night. Now he can spend days alone, finding his way by smell and sound. The wolf he follows waits for him in the trees, then races ahead to show him a trail. Buck turns back to Thornton several times, even when the forest offers food. That choice ends only when the camp is destroyed. After the attack, he pauses by the empty fire and recognizes that Thornton will not call him back again. The wolf is wary of Buck at first. They sniff the air around each other and then run along the same trail. Buck chooses to turn back when he thinks of Thornton waiting at camp.

One day Buck returns and smells danger before he reaches the tents. The camp has been attacked; he finds Thornton and his companions dead. Men from a nearby group are still there, and Buck charges at them. They scatter, but Buck cannot bring Thornton back. He searches the place where his friend lived and waits for a voice that no longer comes. The fire and tents cannot give him a reason to stay. He goes into the trees and meets the wolf again. Buck follows the attackers through the camp before driving them away; their flight leaves a terrible quiet behind. He noses around the place where Thornton once sat, but no one answers him.

Other wolves approach Buck and test him. He fights when they challenge him, then runs with their pack. His strength and knowledge of the forest help him lead them. The people in the region later speak of a large dog moving among wolves. In summer Buck returns to the place where Thornton died. He stands there for a while, then leaves the old camp and follows the pack into the forest. The first wolves do not welcome a stranger at once. Buck has to hold his ground and learn their movements. Later he can run at their head, but the old campsite remains a place he visits alone.

title: Around the World in Eighty Days: A Wager and a Departure
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Phileas Fogg follows an exact daily routine in London. At the Reform Club he reads new travel times for railways and steamships and says a person can circle the world in eighty days. Other members doubt him, so he bets a large sum that he can do it. That evening he leaves with his new servant Passepartout. They travel by train and ship toward Suez, then continue for India. Fogg counts the days carefully and plans each connection. Passepartout had hoped that his new job would be quiet. At the station he finds Fogg ready to leave with a small bag and a large sum of money. They board a train before the servant has time to settle into the household routine. Fogg checks the schedule while Passepartout wonders what the next stop will demand.

Detective Fix watches Fogg at Suez. A bank has been robbed in London, and Fix mistakenly believes the traveller is the thief. He wants an arrest warrant to arrive, but Fogg keeps moving from port to port. Fix follows without telling Fogg why. In India the travellers board a train, expecting the line to carry them across the country. Part of the railway is unfinished. Fogg buys an elephant and hires a guide to take them through the forest to the next station.

During that journey, the party learns that a young woman called Aouda is in danger. Fogg chooses to stop and rescue her, though the delay may cost him the wager. Passepartout helps in the rescue, and they leave with Aouda on the elephant. She has no safe way to remain behind, so the group takes her onward. They reach the railway and continue the journey. Fogg still watches the timetable, but he has spent some of its precious hours helping someone he did not know when he left London.

He listens to Passepartout speak freely about the route and uses each departure to follow them.

Passepartout helps in the rescue, and they leave with Aouda on the elephant. She has no safe way to remain behind, so the group takes her onward. They reach the railway and continue the journey. The guide leads it through forest paths that the travellers could never have found alone. Aouda’s rescue demands a quick decision, and Fogg chooses her safety even while calculating the hours he will lose.

title: Around the World in Eighty Days: Across Asia and the Pacific
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
The travellers reach Calcutta after their journey across India. Passepartout is charged because he entered a temple with his shoes on during an earlier stop. Detective Fix has helped bring the complaint; he wants Fogg delayed until an arrest warrant arrives. Fogg pays the fine so the group can catch its ship. Aouda travels with them to Hong Kong, where they hope to find one of her relatives. The relative has moved away. Fogg invites Aouda to continue with him rather than leave her alone in an unfamiliar port.

Fix still wants to keep Fogg in British territory. He tells Passepartout that he suspects Fogg of stealing from a bank, but the servant does not tell his master. When Fix learns that their next ship will leave earlier than expected, he gives Passepartout drink and keeps him from carrying the news. Passepartout reaches the vessel, but Fogg and Aouda miss it. They go to the quay and find that their servant has vanished with the ship. Fogg hires a smaller boat in rough weather, hoping to catch another connection. He cannot know where Passepartout will land. Passepartout had hoped to protect his master by watching Fix, but the detective uses the servant’s own delay against him. On board, Passepartout looks for Fogg and realizes he has sailed without him. When he reaches Japan, he cannot pay for a room. The performance troupe gives him a temporary place to sleep and a way to continue searching.

Passepartout reaches Yokohama with little money. He looks for food and work while searching for his companions. A performance troupe offers him a place, and he joins its show. Fogg and Aouda arrive by another route and find him there. The three are relieved to be together again, although the separation has cost them time. They prepare to cross the Pacific, still followed by Fix and still facing the deadline of Fogg's wager.
